title: Psychedelia (c. 1965–1969): studios, scenes, and longer songs
dek: After the British Invasion, studios and ballrooms stretched the pop single. San Francisco, London, and a few other cities made longer songs, light shows, and albums you were meant to sit with.
text: Psychedelia (c. 1965–1969): studios, scenes, and longer songs After the British Invasion, studios and ballrooms stretched the pop single. San Francisco, London, and a few other cities made longer songs, light shows, and albums you were meant to sit with. c. 1965–1969 “Psychedelia” is a press and fan word, not a union card. San Francisco ballrooms, London underground clubs, Los Angeles studios, Austin, New York, and São Paulo were not one scene with a shared committee. LSD is part of the history; it is not the whole of the music. This lesson looks out from those rooms and desks. Group Sounds in Japan and Tropicália in Brazil were running in the same years. They are not decoration, and they are not a required Asia pairing. The Velvet Underground is a same-time New York contrast, not a peer assigned by geography. Music music 1965 Rubber Soul / folk-rock The Beatles’ Rubber Soul (UK, 3 December). The Byrds had already put folk songs on electric twelve-string. Ken Kesey’s Acid Tests were running in California. The useful unit was still often a 45. 1966 Studios and ballrooms Pet Sounds (16 May). Revolver (UK, 5 August). The 13th Floor Elevators’ The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators. Bill Graham at the Fillmore; Chet Helms and the Family Dog at the Avalon. UFO opened in London on 23 December. 1967 Monterey / FM / Piper Monterey Pop, 16–18 June. Tom Donahue’s album-cut shows on KMPX-FM in San Francisco. Pink Floyd’s The Piper at the Gates of Dawn (UK, 4 August). Are You Experienced, Surrealistic Pillow, The Velvet Underground & Nico. 1968 Tropicália / AI-5 Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis and Os Mutantes’ debut. Fillmore West opened. Institutional Act No. 5 in Brazil (13 December). Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil were arrested on 27 December. 1969 Woodstock / Altamont Woodstock, 15–18 August, on Max Yasgur’s farm in Bethel, New York. Altamont Speedway, 6 December. Japanese Group Sounds was past its 1967–68 peak. Veloso and Gil left for London. The first song recorded for Revolver was already a studio machine On 6 April 1966, at EMI Studios on Abbey Road, the Beatles began Revolver with John Lennon’s “Tomorrow Never Knows.” Engineer Geoff Emerick ran Lennon’s voice through a Leslie rotating speaker cabinet built for Hammond organs. Several tape loops — including a laughing voice and a distorted guitar — were mixed live on the desk because four-track tape did not leave much room to stack them later. The finished track is under three minutes. The “long song” in 1966 was often still a single’s length. What had changed was the method: the studio was no longer only a place to photograph a live group. psychedelia psychedelic Press and fan word, mid-to-late 1960s, for music, light shows, and graphics associated with longer forms, studio experiment, and, in some crowds, LSD. It was never a single committee or sound. acid rock American name for the guitar-heavy, often improvising end of the San Francisco ballroom circuit. Not a synonym for every London studio experiment. ballroom ballrooms In this lesson, the San Francisco dance halls — Fillmore, Avalon, later Fillmore West — that booked rock bills on a floor without seats, with light shows. A room and a format, not a waltz. FM FM radio underground FM free-form radio Frequency-modulation radio. From 1967, stations such as KMPX in San Francisco used FM to play album cuts instead of AM Top 40 singles. The LP became a radio unit. concept album concept albums An LP meant to be heard as a set, sometimes with a linking idea or running order that is not just a stack of singles. Sgt. Pepper is the usual example; Pet Sounds and Revolver already asked for the same attention. Tropicália Tropicalismo tropicalia Brazilian late-1960s arts movement. Hélio Oiticica used the word for a 1967 installation; Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil applied it to music that mixed Brazilian forms with electric studio pop under a military dictatorship. folk-rock Mid-1960s electric setting of folk repertoire and songwriting, associated in the United States with the Byrds. A bridge from clubs to the later 1960s studio and ballroom records. light show light shows liquid light show Projected oils, dyes, and slides on ballroom and club walls, run with the band. Part of the Fillmore/Avalon and UFO nights, not a music video. festival festivals Here, multi-act outdoor bills that scaled a dance to a fairground or farm: Monterey 1967, Woodstock 1969, Altamont 1969. Logistics and a crowd, not only a vibe. album culture The late-1960s market habit of selling rock as long-playing records, FM time, and gatefold objects rather than only as 45 rpm singles. British Invasion American press name, from 1964, for British beat groups on the U.S. charts. The immediate past of this lesson. See the earlier capsule on that chart event. beat groups beat group British early-1960s guitar-bass-drums-vocals groups. The school many of the later studio bands came from. folk clubs folk club Small rooms where singers learned traditional and contemporary folk songs, often acoustic, before folk-rock and the later 1960s electric bands. amphetamines amphetamine Stimulant drugs. In early-1960s Britain, some Mods and working musicians used them — including Drinamyl tablets nicknamed purple hearts — to stay awake through all-nighters. Short, fast sets fitted that use. Drinamyl purple hearts purple heart British amphetamine–barbiturate tablet. “Purple hearts” was a street name. Part of the Mod all-nighter, not of the later ballroom light show. LSD lysergic acid diethylamide Hallucinogenic drug. Present in some California and London scenes by the mid-1960s. Where it was part of the room, longer sets and light shows fitted better than a three-minute riff. Not an explanation for every record in this lesson. Acid Tests Acid Test Ken Kesey’s 1965–66 California events: a house band, lights, and LSD in warehouses and halls. One local before of the San Francisco dance. Family Dog San Francisco commune and promotion group around Chet Helms. Ran dances at the Avalon Ballroom from 1966. Group Sounds グループ・サウンズ GS Japanese mid-1960s electric-guitar pop. Peaked 1967–68; fading by 1969–70 as folk and harder rock took students. Same years as this lesson, not an assigned twin of San Francisco. kayōkyoku Japanese popular song of the postwar decades, the domestic tradition Group Sounds bands heard alongside imported beat records. Exploding Plastic Inevitable EPI Andy Warhol’s 1966–67 multimedia events, with the Velvet Underground. New York’s live context for that group, not a Fillmore dance. anthropophagy Oswald de Andrade’s 1928 idea of Brazil “eating” foreign culture. Tropicália musicians used it as a way to mix Beatles records with Brazilian forms without pretending to be a cover band. Institutional Act No. 5 AI-5 AI5 Brazilian decree, 13 December 1968, that hardened military censorship and repression. The political weather of Tropicália’s last months as a public movement. four-track four-track tape 4-track Tape format used at Abbey Road for Revolver: four discrete tracks. Loops and overdubs had to be planned or mixed live because there was little spare space. Leslie speaker Leslie Leslie cabinet Rotating speaker cabinet built for Hammond organs. Geoff Emerick ran John Lennon’s voice through one on “Tomorrow Never Knows.” A hardware fact. tape loop tape loops A length of recording tape joined end to end so a sound repeats. Several loops were mixed live into “Tomorrow Never Knows.” Wrecking Crew Informal name for the Los Angeles session players Brian Wilson used on Pet Sounds. They were studio professionals, not the touring Beach Boys lineup on those tracks. hard rock Louder, riff-based rock that is one line out of Hendrix, the Who, and the heavier ballroom nights. This lesson names it as an after, not as a syllabus. Haight-Ashbury Haight San Francisco neighborhood at Haight and Ashbury streets, the 1967 press address for the local counterculture. Sidewalks and crash pads; the ballrooms were elsewhere in the city. Fillmore Fillmore Auditorium the Fillmore Ballroom at Fillmore and Geary, San Francisco. Bill Graham began booking rock dances there in 1966. Fillmore West Graham’s larger San Francisco room from 1968, in the former Carousel Ballroom. Not the original Fillmore Auditorium. Avalon Ballroom Avalon Dance hall at Sutter and Van Ness, San Francisco. Family Dog / Chet Helms shows, 1966–69. UFO Club UFO London underground club opened 23 December 1966 by Joe Boyd and John Hopkins at 31 Tottenham Court Road. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine played the first night. Moved to the Roundhouse in 1967 and folded that autumn. Roundhouse the Roundhouse Circular former railway building in Chalk Farm, London. UFO’s second address in 1967. Abbey Road EMI Studios Abbey Road Studios EMI’s London studios on Abbey Road. Revolver and The Piper at the Gates of Dawn were recorded there. Western Recorders Western Hollywood studio where much of Pet Sounds was tracked, with engineer Chuck Britz among the staff. Gold Star Gold Star Studios Hollywood studio associated with Phil Spector and used for some Beach Boys dates around Pet Sounds. KMPX KMPX-FM San Francisco FM station where Tom Donahue began playing album-cut rock in 1967. An origin point for underground FM. KSAN KSAN-FM San Francisco FM station that took Donahue’s staff after the KMPX strike. Broadcast a long call-in after Altamont. Monterey International Pop Festival Monterey Pop Monterey Monterey Pop Festival Non-profit festival at the Monterey County Fairgrounds, 16–18 June 1967. Otis Redding, Ravi Shankar, the Who, Hendrix, Airplane, Joplin, and others. Filmed by D. A. Pennebaker. Woodstock Woodstock Music and Art Fair Woodstock Festival Festival on Max Yasgur’s farm in Bethel, New York, 15–18 August 1969. The end-edge of this lesson’s festival story, not its beginning. Altamont Altamont Speedway Altamont Free Concert Free Rolling Stones concert at Altamont Speedway, California, 6 December 1969. Crowding, fights, and the killing of Meredith Hunter. A logistics failure at highway scale. Summer of Love Press name for San Francisco, especially Haight-Ashbury, in 1967. A crowd and a headline, not a recording technique. Radio 1 BBC Radio 1 BBC pop network launched in 1967 as official radio for a habit pirate ships had already trained. British context for the same years as UFO and Piper. BBC British public broadcaster. Needle-time still shaped how many records it could play in the mid-1960s; Radio 1 was part of the 1967 answer. The Beatles Beatles Liverpool group, then Abbey Road. Rubber Soul, Revolver, and Sgt. Pepper are the studio facts in this lesson, not another invasion-era television date. The Beach Boys Beach Boys California group. Pet Sounds (1966) is Brian Wilson’s studio answer to Rubber Soul, made largely with session players. The Byrds Byrds Los Angeles group. Folk-rock on electric twelve-string; “Eight Miles High” (1966) is their usual bridge into this lesson’s years. Jefferson Airplane Airplane San Francisco group. Surrealistic Pillow (1967) put Grace Slick’s “White Rabbit” on the radio while the band still played the ballrooms. Grateful Dead the Dead San Francisco group. Ballroom improvisation as a method; the long set rather than the three-minute single. Big Brother and the Holding Company Big Brother San Francisco group. Janis Joplin sang with them from 1966 until 1968. Cheap Thrills is the 1968 album; Monterey is the 1967 live introduction for many viewers. Janis Joplin Joplin American singer. With Big Brother at Monterey; later a solo name. A ballroom and festival fact in this lesson, not a studio-tape story. Jimi Hendrix Hendrix American guitarist who became famous in London with the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Are You Experienced (1967); Monterey, 18 June 1967, where he destroyed a Stratocaster. The Jimi Hendrix Experience Jimi Hendrix Experience the Experience Hendrix, Noel Redding, Mitch Mitchell. London-based trio, 1966–69. The records were London studio jobs; Monterey made the American name. Pink Floyd London group. House band at UFO in early 1967; The Piper at the Gates of Dawn recorded at Abbey Road and released 4 August 1967, mostly written by Syd Barrett. Soft Machine Canterbury/London group. Played UFO’s opening night with Pink Floyd. Jazz-leaning, not a San Francisco ballroom band. Traffic British group, formed 1967. Mr. Fantasy (late 1967) is a UK studio and cottage fact, not a Fillmore franchise. 13th Floor Elevators the Elevators Austin group. The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators (1966) put the word on the sleeve early, with Roky Erickson and an amplified jug. Love Los Angeles group around Arthur Lee. Forever Changes (November 1967, Elektra) is orchestral folk-rock from that city, not from Haight-Ashbury. The Velvet Underground Velvet Underground VU New York group. The Velvet Underground & Nico (March 1967) and Warhol’s Exploding Plastic Inevitable. A same-time contrast, not the West Coast’s missing conscience. Os Mutantes São Paulo group (Sérgio Dias, Arnaldo Baptista, Rita Lee). Debut album 1968; “Panis et Circenses” opens it. Tropicália’s electric band, not a Beatles tribute act. The Who Who London group. Smashed instruments at Monterey, the theatre Hendrix then had to outdo. Not a San Francisco band. The Rolling Stones Rolling Stones the Stones London group. Headlined the Altamont free concert, 6 December 1969. In this lesson they are that date, not the 1964 Invasion story. The Tigers Tigers Japanese Group Sounds band, a television name at GS’s 1967–68 peak. Otis Redding American soul singer. Played Monterey, 1967. On the bill to show that the festival was not only the local ballroom bands. Ravi Shankar Indian sitar player. Played Monterey, 1967. A full set of Hindustani classical music on a pop-festival bill, not a studio garnish. Brian Wilson Beach Boys writer and producer. Pet Sounds is his studio project with Tony Asher and Los Angeles session players. Tony Asher Lyricist who worked with Brian Wilson on Pet Sounds. George Martin Parlophone/EMI producer for the Beatles. Revolver is a staff-producer record at a major-label studio, not a bedroom experiment. Geoff Emerick Abbey Road engineer on Revolver. Close-miked drums; Leslie cabinet on Lennon’s voice; tape loops mixed live. John Lennon Beatles writer and singer. “Tomorrow Never Knows” is his Revolver track; the vocal is a Leslie cabinet, not a metaphor. Paul McCartney Beatles writer. On the Monterey festival board; insisted the Jimi Hendrix Experience be booked. Bill Graham San Francisco promoter. Fillmore Auditorium from 1966; Fillmore West from 1968. A lease and a door, not a commune. Chet Helms Family Dog promoter. Avalon Ballroom from 1966. Recruited Janis Joplin to Big Brother. Joe Boyd American producer in London. Co-founded UFO with John Hopkins in 1966. John Hopkins Hoppy Hoppy Hopkins London underground organizer. Co-founded UFO; connected to International Times and the 1960s London press scene. Tom Donahue Disc jockey and promoter. Began album-cut rock on KMPX-FM in San Francisco in 1967; later KSAN. Underground FM as a format. Syd Barrett Pink Floyd’s original writer and guitarist. Most of The Piper at the Gates of Dawn is his. The later Floyd is another lesson. Grace Slick Jefferson Airplane singer from 1966. Brought “White Rabbit” and “Somebody to Love” from her previous group, the Great Society. Great Society the Great Society Grace Slick’s San Francisco group before Jefferson Airplane. Source of “White Rabbit.” Roky Erickson 13th Floor Elevators singer. Austin, not San Francisco. Arthur Lee Love’s singer and writer. Forever Changes is his 1967 Los Angeles record. Andy Warhol New York artist. Produced and packaged The Velvet Underground & Nico; ran the Exploding Plastic Inevitable. Nico German singer on The Velvet Underground & Nico. A voice on that album, not a San Francisco ballroom name. Gilberto Gil Gil Brazilian musician, Tropicália. Co-organized the 1968 manifesto album; arrested 27 December 1968; exiled to London in 1969. Caetano Veloso Veloso Brazilian musician, Tropicália. Took Oiticica’s word for a song; arrested with Gil in December 1968; London exile 1969. Gal Costa Brazilian singer on Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis (1968). Tom Zé Brazilian musician on the Tropicália manifesto album. Rogério Duprat Brazilian arranger on Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis and Os Mutantes’ debut. Studio craft, not a light show. Hélio Oiticica Brazilian artist. His 1967 Rio installation Tropicália gave the movement its name: penetrable structures, plants, sand, a television. Oswald de Andrade Brazilian writer. His 1928 idea of cultural anthropophagy was reused by Tropicália musicians in 1967–68. Ken Kesey American writer. Organized the Acid Tests in California, 1965–66. D. A. Pennebaker Pennebaker Filmmaker. Monterey Pop (1968) is the licensed documentary of the 1967 festival. Chas Chandler Former Animals bassist; produced the Jimi Hendrix Experience’s early London records. Noel Redding Bassist in the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Mitch Mitchell Drummer in the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Max Yasgur Dairy farmer in Bethel, New York, whose land hosted Woodstock in August 1969. Meredith Hunter Eighteen-year-old killed at Altamont on 6 December 1969, in front of the stage. A fact of that concert, not a symbol to decorate a paragraph. Arnold Skolnick Designer of the 1969 Woodstock bird-and-guitar advertisement poster. Phil Spector American producer. Wall of Sound method Wilson was expanding, not copying, on Pet Sounds. Bob Dylan Dylan American songwriter. His electric turn is a different chapter; named here only as the folk-to-electric bridge other people were also on. Mods Mod British youth style of the early-to-mid 1960s. All-nighters and, for some, amphetamines. The tempo before the light show. Capitol Capitol Records American label. Issued Pet Sounds and, in the United States, the Beatles. Parlophone EMI label that issued the Beatles in Britain, including Rubber Soul and Revolver. RCA RCA Victor Label that issued Jefferson Airplane’s Surrealistic Pillow. Elektra Elektra Records Label that issued Love’s Forever Changes. Verve Label that issued The Velvet Underground & Nico. International Artists Houston label that issued The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators. Track Records Track UK label that issued Are You Experienced in May 1967. Reprise US label that issued Are You Experienced in August 1967 with a different track list and cover. Warner US label that issued the Grateful Dead’s debut album in 1967. Rubber Soul Beatles album, UK release 3 December 1965. The LP Brian Wilson heard as a whole and answered with Pet Sounds. Revolver Beatles album, UK release 5 August 1966. Four-track Abbey Road, Martin and Emerick. Studio method before Sgt. Pepper’s costumes. Pet Sounds Beach Boys album, Capitol, 16 May 1966. Produced by Brian Wilson with session players in Hollywood. Sgt. Pepper Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band Beatles album, May 1967. The usual concept-album example. This lesson treats the 1966 pair as the clearer method. Tomorrow Never Knows Lennon song on Revolver. First track recorded for the album, 6 April 1966. Leslie vocal, tape loops mixed live. Under three minutes. God Only Knows Beach Boys song on Pet Sounds, 1966. Wilson–Asher. A short song whose arrangement is the studio fact. White Rabbit Jefferson Airplane single and Surrealistic Pillow track, 1967. Written by Grace Slick. Bolero-like build; AM radio length. Somebody to Love Jefferson Airplane single from Surrealistic Pillow, 1967. Also brought by Grace Slick from the Great Society. Are You Experienced Jimi Hendrix Experience debut. UK, Track, May 1967; US, Reprise, August 1967, with a different running order that added the early singles. Purple Haze Hendrix single, 1967. On the US Are You Experienced. Two and a half minutes. Official audio exists; the Monterey fire is a different document. The Piper at the Gates of Dawn Piper at the Gates of Dawn Piper Pink Floyd debut, UK 4 August 1967, Abbey Road, mostly Syd Barrett. The studio record of the UFO band. See Emily Play Pink Floyd UK single, 16 June 1967. Official channel upload. Later on the US Piper. A three-minute underground 45. Arnold Layne Pink Floyd’s first UK single, 1967. UFO-era 45, before Piper. Surrealistic Pillow Jefferson Airplane album, RCA, 1 February 1967. First with Grace Slick and Spencer Dryden in the lineup that became the radio version of the band. Forever Changes Love album, Elektra, November 1967. Arthur Lee, Los Angeles, orchestral arrangements. Not a Haight-Ashbury record. The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators The Psychedelic Sounds 13th Floor Elevators album, International Artists, 1966. The word “psychedelic” as a sleeve fact before the Summer of Love headline. You’re Gonna Miss Me You're Gonna Miss Me 13th Floor Elevators track and single, on the 1966 International Artists album. The Velvet Underground & Nico Debut album, Verve, 12 March 1967. Recorded 1966. Warhol packaging. New York, same calendar as Surrealistic Pillow and Piper. Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis Tropicália ou Panis et Circencis Panis et Circencis 1968 Brazilian collaborative album organized by Veloso and Gil. Manifesto record of musical Tropicália. Panis et Circenses Panis Et Circenses Panis et circenses Veloso–Gil song. Opens Os Mutantes’ 1968 debut; also on the Tropicália manifesto album. Studio shape-shifting in Portuguese. Eight Miles High Byrds single, 1966. Folk-rock group stretching form and modal guitar in the same year as Pet Sounds and Revolver. Mr. Fantasy Traffic album, UK late 1967. British, not a San Francisco export. Cheap Thrills Big Brother and the Holding Company album, 1968, with Janis Joplin. After Monterey; still a San Francisco group record. Eleanor Rigby Beatles song on Revolver. String octet, no Beatles playing as a beat group. A studio fact on the same LP as the tape loops. Wild Thing Song Hendrix closed with at Monterey, 18 June 1967, before destroying the Stratocaster. The theatre, not the studio method. Monterey Pop D. A. Pennebaker’s 1968 documentary of the Monterey festival. Licensed editions exist; it is a film, not a bootleg tape. International Times IT London underground newspaper. Part of the print culture around UFO. San Francisco Oracle Oracle the Oracle Haight-Ashbury underground paper, 1966–68. Psychedelic lettering as print, not only as posters. San Francisco Mime Troupe Political theatre company. Bill Graham’s benefit shows for them in 1965 led him to the Fillmore. Carousel Ballroom San Francisco room that became Fillmore West when Graham moved there in 1968. Bethel Town in New York State. Woodstock the festival was on Yasgur’s farm here, not in the town of Woodstock. Tottenham Court Road London street. UFO’s first address was the basement at number 31, from December 1966 to July 1967. Bahia Brazilian state. Veloso and Gil came from there before São Paulo and the Tropicália records. São Paulo Brazilian city where Tropicália musicians met Os Mutantes and used television song festivals as a public stage. Austin Texas city. Home of the 13th Floor Elevators. Not a suburb of the Fillmore. Before Beat groups, folk clubs, and a change of tempo The British Invasion of 1964–65 had already sold America a British version of American rhythm and blues and rock and roll. From Britain the same years were still a 45 rpm business: beat groups, package tours, pirate ships around a BBC that limited how many records it could play, and folk and R&B clubs where a singer learned other people’s songs before writing. The Byrds in Los Angeles put folk repertoire on electric twelve-string and called it folk-rock. Bob Dylan’s electric turn is a different chapter. The useful fact here is the bridge: acoustic clubs and beat cellars were the school; the next records asked for more time on the disc and more time in the room. The chemical history is narrower than the posters later claimed. In early-1960s Britain, some Mods and working musicians used amphetamines — Drinamyl tablets nicknamed purple hearts among them — to stay awake through all-nighters. The music that fit that use was short, loud, and built to keep a floor moving. Lysergic acid diethylamide, LSD, was an older laboratory compound that a smaller set of writers and musicians in California and London were taking by the mid-1960s. Ken Kesey’s Acid Tests, from 1965, put a house band, lights, and the drug in the same warehouses. What changed in some scenes was tempo and length, not a sudden moral collapse. A three-minute riff and a thirty-minute jam are different jobs. Amphetamines helped with the first. LSD, where it was part of the room, fitted the second: light shows that did not need a verse-chorus to land, and sets that could wander. Not every group used either. The Grateful Dead’s long improvisations and the Beatles’ tape loops are not the same practice. Treat the drug shift as a real historical change in some crowds, and as a poor explanation for every sitar on a B-side. Rubber Soul, released in the United Kingdom on 3 December 1965, is the album that made that change audible on a major label without yet wearing the later costume. Brian Wilson heard it as a whole LP, not a stack of singles, and went into Western Recorders and Gold Star in Los Angeles to answer it. The Beatles, for their part, were about to stop touring and treat Abbey Road as the instrument. Folk clubs and beat groups got them there. The next two years would be studios, ballrooms, and a press word — psychedelia — that tried to name too many rooms at once. The era Studios, ballrooms, FM, and a weekend in Monterey Two kinds of room did most of the work: the recording studio and the dance hall. In Hollywood, Brian Wilson produced Pet Sounds with lyricist Tony Asher and the session players later nicknamed the Wrecking Crew. Capitol released the album on 16 May 1966. Wilson was not taking the Beach Boys on the road as a self-contained instrumental band for those tracks. He was stacking voices and unusual instruments the way Phil Spector had stacked a wall of sound, then going further into quiet, bass harmonica, and dog barks. In London, from April to June 1966, the Beatles recorded Revolver at EMI Studios on Abbey Road with George Martin and a young engineer, Geoff Emerick. They were still on four-track tape. Automatic double tracking, close-miked drums, tape loops, and a Leslie cabinet on a vocal were hardware solutions, not metaphors. Revolver appeared in the United Kingdom on 5 August 1966. The two albums did not cause each other. They were made in the same months, in different buildings, by people who were listening to one another’s finished records. EMI Studios, Abbey Road, photographed in 2005. Revolver was recorded here in 1966, on four-track tape, with George Martin producing and Geoff Emerick engineering. The zebra crossing on the album sleeve is a later photograph. The building is the 1966 fact. The white Georgian front of Abbey Road Studios in London, with a parked car and the famous zebra crossing out of frame to the left. San Francisco’s contribution was not first a studio method. It was a circuit of ballrooms. Bill Graham, who had managed the San Francisco Mime Troupe, began putting on rock dances at the Fillmore Auditorium at Fillmore and Geary in 1966. Chet Helms and the Family Dog took the Avalon Ballroom at Sutter and Van Ness. For a few weeks they had shared the Fillmore on alternate nights; then Graham leased the room and Helms moved. The format was Friday and Saturday, several bands, two sets each, a floor without seats, and a liquid light show on the walls. Jefferson Airplane, the Grateful Dead, and Big Brother and the Holding Company — Janis Joplin joined Big Brother in 1966 — were local bills before they were national names. The posters on the telephone poles were the weekly newspaper: hard to read on purpose, sold afterward as objects. This lesson does not reproduce those posters. Many are still in copyright. The rooms are the evidence that survives without piracy. 1268 and 1244 Sutter Street, March 2022, the former Avalon Ballroom. Family Dog dances ran here from 1966 to 1969. The light show and the $2.50 at the top of the stairs are gone. The upstairs hall is why the address still matters. A three-story white commercial building on Sutter Street, San Francisco, with two street-level entrances and a faded painted sign high on the wall. San Francisco Oracle, volume 1, number 5, January 1967. The Haight-Ashbury underground paper used the same dense, hard-to-scan lettering as the ballroom posters. This cover announced a gathering in Golden Gate Park. The Oracle is a document of the scene’s print culture, not a concert ticket. January 1967 cover of the San Francisco Oracle: ornate lettering around a photograph of a gathering in Golden Gate Park, with names including Timothy Leary and Allen Ginsberg. London’s version was smaller and shorter. Joe Boyd and John “Hoppy” Hopkins opened the UFO Club on 23 December 1966 in the basement of 31 Tottenham Court Road, under an Irish dance hall. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine played the opening night. The bills mixed bands with light shows, films, and poetry. International Times and the rest of the underground press treated UFO as a weekly address. The landlord ended the Tottenham Court Road residency in July 1967 after a tabloid scare; the club moved to the Roundhouse in Chalk Farm and folded that autumn. Pink Floyd’s The Piper at the Gates of Dawn, with Syd Barrett writing most of it, was recorded at Abbey Road and released in the United Kingdom on 4 August 1967. Arnold Layne and See Emily Play were still singles. The British underground could be a three-minute 45 and a late club in the same month. The Roundhouse, Chalk Farm Road, photographed in 2006. UFO moved here from Tottenham Court Road in the summer of 1967 and did not last the year. The building is a former railway turntable shed. In 1966–67 it was one of the few London rooms that could hold the underground’s light show and a band at once. The circular brick Roundhouse in Camden, London, seen from Chalk Farm Road with traffic in the foreground. Radio had to catch up with the length. AM Top 40 still wanted three minutes. In April 1967, Tom Donahue began playing album cuts on KMPX-FM in San Francisco, a small station that had been filling hours with foreign-language shows. Within months the format — no jingles, album sides, records the singles chart did not know what to do with — had a name, underground FM, and copies in other cities. The LP, not the 45, became a radio unit. Concept albums and FM were a pair: Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band (May 1967) is the usual example, but the habit of sitting through a side was already being trained on Pet Sounds, Revolver, and the San Francisco records that did not fade at 2:30. Monterey, 16–18 June 1967, was the weekend the California scene rented a fairground and invited the rest of the touring world. The Monterey International Pop Festival was organized as a non-profit. Artists played for expenses. The bill was not only San Francisco: Otis Redding, Ravi Shankar, the Who, the Jimi Hendrix Experience, Jefferson Airplane, Big Brother and Janis Joplin. Paul McCartney, on the festival board, had insisted Hendrix be booked. D. A. Pennebaker filmed it. The Summer of Love, that same season in Haight-Ashbury, is the press name for the crowd that followed. The useful Monterey fact is the booking: soul, Indian classical music, London guitar theatre, and the local ballroom bands on one weekend, before Woodstock made the festival itself the product. Cash Box, 29 April 1967, page 20. A trade-paper advertisement for Monterey, weeks before the fairground opened. The type is a booking list, not a psychedelic poster. The names are the evidence: this was sold to the industry as an international pop festival, not as a private San Francisco dance. Black-and-white 1967 Cash Box advertisement for the Monterey International Pop Festival, listing dates and a long roster of acts. The Greenville News, 30 April 1967, reprinting an Associated Press picture from Haight-Ashbury. National papers were already touring the neighborhood that spring. The photograph is a wire-service document of a sidewalk, not a concert. Treat the caption’s language as 1967 press, not as a definition of the music. 1967 newspaper photograph of a crowd of young people sitting and standing on a Haight-Ashbury sidewalk, with a short news caption about hippies. United States and United Kingdom were not interchangeable. American psychedelia had ballrooms, FM album radio, and, by 1967–69, festivals that tried to scale a dance to a field. British psychedelia had a short-lived club, an official pop network (BBC Radio 1, 1967) that arrived as the pirates were squeezed, and a studio culture in which the Beatles and Pink Floyd could treat Abbey Road as a lab while still issuing singles. Traffic, from Birmingham, made Mr. Fantasy at the end of 1967 without being a San Francisco franchise. The word “psychedelia” covered both. The jobs in the room were different: a Fillmore night was a dance with lights; a Revolver session was a desk, a tape machine, and a clock. The field Many names, and three rooms to slow down in A gallery of three faces is the wrong picture. Name the field, then slow down. The Beatles and the Beach Boys in the studio. The Byrds. Jefferson Airplane and the Grateful Dead. Janis Joplin with Big Brother and the Holding Company. Jimi Hendrix. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine. Traffic. The 13th Floor Elevators in Austin. Love in Los Angeles. The Velvet Underground in New York. In Brazil, Gilberto Gil, Caetano Veloso, Os Mutantes. The Who and Otis Redding pass through Monterey. Bill Graham and Chet Helms ran the San Francisco doors. Joe Boyd and Hoppy Hopkins ran UFO. Tom Donahue moved albums onto FM. George Martin and Geoff Emerick sat at the Abbey Road desk; Brian Wilson sat at Western. Syd Barrett, Grace Slick, Roky Erickson, Arthur Lee, Andy Warhol and Nico. Hélio Oiticica’s installation gave Tropicália a name before the records did. That is a crowd on purpose. Pet Sounds and Revolver are the studio method at full size. Wilson, not touring those tracks as a five-piece, used Hollywood session players and Capitol’s budget to make an album whose quiet is as deliberate as its hooks. “God Only Knows” is a two-minute-fifty song with a bass line that does not behave like surf. The Beatles, four-track and restless, made Revolver a catalogue of tricks that other engineers could copy: backwards tape, a string octet on “Eleanor Rigby,” a vocal that sounds as if it is spinning because it is spinning inside a Leslie. Sgt. Pepper, the next year, is the record the syllabuses never let go. The 1966 pair is the better evidence of method, because the costumes had not yet become the story. The San Francisco ballroom circuit is the live method. Fillmore and Avalon, then Fillmore West in 1968 when Graham moved into the former Carousel Ballroom. Light shows, posters, and bills that ran past midnight. Airplane’s Surrealistic Pillow (February 1967) put “White Rabbit” and “Somebody to Love” on AM; the same band could still play a ballroom set that did not sound like a singles revue. The Dead treated the night as improvisation. Big Brother, with Joplin, were louder and shorter. Acid rock is the American press name for the guitar-heavy end of that circuit. It is not a synonym for every London studio experiment. The circuit also had a door price, a lease, and a promoter who could lose the room. Graham’s Fillmore and Helms’s Avalon were businesses in disagreement, not a commune with two addresses. Tropicália is a contemporaneous case, not an exotic footnote. In April 1967, at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro, Hélio Oiticica showed an installation he called Tropicália: penetrable structures, plants, sand, a television. Caetano Veloso took the word for a song. In 1968 Veloso and Gilberto Gil organized the collaborative album Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis, with Os Mutantes, Gal Costa, Tom Zé, and arrangements by Rogério Duprat. Os Mutantes’ own debut the same year opened with “Panis et Circenses,” a Veloso–Gil song that changes shape the way a Beatles track from 1967 changes shape, in Portuguese, with Brazilian rhythm and studio jokes. This was not San Francisco exported. It was Bahia and São Paulo musicians using electric guitars, tropical kitsch, and Oswald de Andrade’s older idea of anthropophagy — eating foreign forms — under a military dictatorship. Institutional Act No. 5, on 13 December 1968, hardened censorship. Veloso and Gil were arrested on 27 December, detained, then pushed toward exile. They left for London in 1969. The records and the arrests are the same years as Monterey and Abbey Road. The police are the local fact. Hendrix is the transatlantic object lesson. He was an American guitarist who became famous in London with Noel Redding and Mitch Mitchell as the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Are You Experienced was issued in the United Kingdom in May 1967. At Monterey on 18 June he closed with “Wild Thing,” set a Fender Stratocaster on fire, and smashed it. A fragment of that guitar — jack, wiring, painted wood — has been exhibited as an object. The theatre was borrowed from the Who, who had already wrecked instruments that weekend. The career was not only the fire: Chas Chandler produced the records in London; American FM then carried the LP. Purple Haze is a two-and-a-half-minute single. The legend is longer than the track. Fragment of the Stratocaster Jimi Hendrix destroyed at Monterey on 18 June 1967, photographed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2019 (loan from MoPOP, Seattle). The object is wood, metal, and nail polish. The film of the fire is still under copyright. This piece of the guitar is what a museum can show without pirating the footage. A charred, painted fragment of a Fender Stratocaster body, showing the input jack and part of the control cavity, displayed in a museum case. Elsewhere The same years, not a ranking of scenes In Japan, Group Sounds — the mid-1960s electric-guitar boom that had heard the Beatles and kayōkyoku at once — peaked in 1967–68 with acts such as the Tigers still on television. By 1969 major members were leaving; by about 1970 the boom was over. Folk and a harder “new rock” were already taking the students who had bought GS singles. That is a fade in the same years as Fillmore West, not an Asian psychedelic twin assigned to match San Francisco. Some Japanese musicians were already looking past the beat-group format. This lesson does not invent a Tokyo UFO to keep the map tidy. In New York, the Velvet Underground recorded with Nico in 1966 and released The Velvet Underground & Nico in March 1967, with Andy Warhol’s banana on the sleeve and the Exploding Plastic Inevitable as the live context. The Factory was not Haight-Ashbury. The songs were about a different set of streets and a different set of drugs. Treat the album as contemporaneous, not as the West Coast’s missing conscience. Love’s Forever Changes, from Los Angeles in November 1967, is another local fact: Arthur Lee, orchestral folk-rock, paranoia in the arrangements, Elektra Records. The 13th Floor Elevators, from Austin, had already put the word on a sleeve in 1966 — The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators — with Roky Erickson and an amplified jug. Texas was not a suburb of the Fillmore. Brazil’s Tropicália, already slowed down above, belongs in this list as a same-time industry: television song festivals, a collaborative LP, a dictatorship, and then London exile. It used some of the same Beatles records the rest of the world used. It was not a cover band for Revolver. The honest comparison is the calendar, not a contest over who was more psychedelic. After Woodstock, Altamont, and rock as album culture Woodstock, 15–18 August 1969, on Max Yasgur’s dairy farm in Bethel, New York, is the end-edge of this lesson’s festival story, not a beginning. Hundreds of thousands of people arrived at a site that had not been built for them. Hendrix played on the morning of the 18th. The Arnold Skolnick poster — a bird on a guitar neck, three days of peace and music — is the image that survived. The music business learned that a field, a sound system, and an LP culture could be a market. It also learned that the market could lose control of the gate. Arnold Skolnick’s 1969 advertisement for the Woodstock Music and Art Fair. Published in the United States without a copyright notice, it is in the public domain there. The bird is a graphic, not a photograph of the farm. Bethel, not the town of Woodstock, is where the stages stood. Woodstock 1969 poster: white bird on a guitar against a red field, with the words 3 Days of Peace & Music and the festival dates. The crowd at Woodstock waiting out rain, August 1969. Photograph by Derek Redmond and Paul Campbell. The popular picture of the weekend is mud. Saturday was also sun. Either way the fact is scale: a dance hall idea stretched until the fence failed. A dense crowd at Woodstock sitting on a hillside under grey sky, many wrapped against rain, the stage distant. Altamont Speedway, on 6 December 1969, was a free Rolling Stones concert in northern California that ended in crowding, fights, and the killing of Meredith Hunter in front of the stage. KSAN-FM, the San Francisco underground station that had inherited Tom Donahue’s staff from KMPX, put callers on the air the next day. The useful historical point is not a sermon. It is that the ballroom’s security, lights, and door could not be improvised at highway scale. The 1960s festival was already a logistics problem. What remained in the shops was album culture. Rock, as a market category, sold long-playing records, gatefold sleeves, and FM time. Hard rock — louder, riff-based, less interested in the light show — is one line out of Hendrix, the Who, and the heavier San Francisco nights. That line continues into the next decade. A later reaction would treat the album, the solo, and the festival as the things to refuse. That reaction becomes punk. It is not this lesson. The 1965–69 story ends with a longer song, a larger crowd, and a business that had learned to bill the LP as the work. A question A question to keep asking If the unit of the music changes from a three-minute 45 to a side of an LP, who is being asked to sit still, and who is being paid for the extra time? Monterey Pop (D. A. Pennebaker, 1968) Pennebaker’s documentary of the June 1967 festival. Licensed home-video editions exist; this is the catalogue record, not a bootleg upload of the film. The Beatles — Tomorrow Never Knows (1966) Revolver, recorded at EMI Studios, Abbey Road. Official Beatles/UMG upload of the studio recording. Lennon’s vocal through a Leslie speaker; tape loops in the mix. If the file moves, search the title on the Beatles’ official channel. The Beach Boys — God Only Knows (1966) Pet Sounds, Capitol. Official Beach Boys channel. This upload is a later video cut to the 1966 studio recording, not a 1966 television clip. Jefferson Airplane — White Rabbit (1967) Surrealistic Pillow, RCA. Official audio on the Jefferson Airplane channel. Grace Slick brought the song from her previous group, the Great Society. The Jimi Hendrix Experience — Purple Haze (1967) Official audio, Experience Hendrix/VEVO. UK single 1967; on the US edition of Are You Experienced. Not the Monterey film. Pink Floyd — See Emily Play (1967) UK single, 16 June 1967, the weekend of Monterey. Official Pink Floyd channel. Later added to the US edition of The Piper at the Gates of Dawn. A three-minute underground record, not a ballroom jam. Os Mutantes — Panis et Circenses (1968) YouTube Topic upload provided by Universal Music Ltda from the 1968 Polydor/Philips-family master. Written by Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil; arranged with Rogério Duprat. Not a 1968 television clip. 13th Floor Elevators — You’re Gonna Miss Me (1966) YouTube Topic upload of the International Artists recording, provided by The Orchard. From The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators. If it moves, search the title plus International Artists.

subject: feminism
title: Second Wave (c. 1963–1982): the personal is political
dek: After the vote, public feminism turned to housework, sex, pay, and who counted as a woman. A bestseller, small consciousness-raising groups, new laws, and a 1977 Black feminist statement made those private facts into politics.
text: Second Wave (c. 1963–1982): the personal is political After the vote, public feminism turned to housework, sex, pay, and who counted as a woman. A bestseller, small consciousness-raising groups, new laws, and a 1977 Black feminist statement made those private facts into politics. c. 1963–1982 “Second wave” is a later Anglo-American classroom name, not what most of the people in this lesson called themselves. The dates are a convenience: The Feminine Mystique (1963) at one end, the Equal Rights Amendment’s extended ratification deadline (30 June 1982) at the other. The United States is the spine because the numbering is. Other countries’ 1960s–70s feminisms are contemporaneous — not copies of an American original. Feminism feminism 1963 Mystique / pay Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique. The Equal Pay Act the same year. A bestseller and a statute; neither was the whole cause. 1966 NOW National Organization for Women founded in Washington, 30 June, after a conference of status-of-women commissions. Friedan first president; Pauli Murray among the founders. 1968 Atlantic City New York Radical Women protest the Miss America pageant, 7 September. Freedom Trash Can. No fire. 1970 Books / strike / Ruskin Sexual Politics; The Dialectic of Sex; Notes from the Second Year; Our Bodies, Ourselves as newsprint; Women’s Strike for Equality, 26 August; first UK Women’s Liberation conference at Ruskin College. 1972–73 Statute / Roe Title IX in the Education Amendments of 1972 (signed 23 June). ERA sent to the states. Ms. magazine. Roe v. Wade decided 22 January 1973. 1977 Combahee / Houston Combahee River Collective Statement (April). National Women’s Conference in Houston (November), and a conservative Pro-Family rally in the same city. 1982 Deadline ERA ratification deadline expires 30 June, three states short. Reagan already in office; Thatcher since 1979. The later names — third wave, intersectionality — are not yet the ones in use. There was no fire on the boardwalk On 7 September 1968, New York Radical Women put bras, girdles, high heels, curlers, and women’s magazines into a “Freedom Trash Can” outside the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City. They asked the city for a permit to burn the contents. The permit was refused: the boardwalk is wood. Nothing was burned. Newspapers, then Art Buchwald’s column, reported a bra-burning anyway. The trash can is the event. The bonfire is the copy. second wave Second Wave second-wave A later Anglo-American label for a span of feminist organizing roughly from the early 1960s through the early 1980s. Most people in it did not use the phrase at the time. It is a later name, not a membership card. doldrums A later name for organized U.S. feminism between the vote and the 1960s: the coalition that had fought for suffrage thinned. It describes one public current going quiet. It does not mean women stopped working, studying, or arguing. the feminine mystique feminine mystique Friedan’s name for the postwar middle-class story that a woman’s fulfillment was husband, children, and house. She treated it as an ideology with a sales force — magazines, advertising, experts — not as a private mood. the problem that has no name Friedan’s phrase in The Feminine Mystique for the dissatisfaction of college-educated housewives who had done what they were told and still felt empty. It named a specific class of unhappiness. It did not name every woman’s. The Feminine Mystique Betty Friedan’s 1963 book, published by W. W. Norton. A survey of her Smith College classmates and a polemic against the house-as-destiny. A public starting point. Not a census of American women. Betty Friedan Friedan American writer (1921–2006). The Feminine Mystique (1963); first president of NOW (1966). She later used the phrase “lavender menace” about lesbians in the movement — a split, not a footnote. Equal Pay Act U.S. statute signed 10 June 1963. It required equal pay for equal work on the basis of sex, with exceptions. A workplace law in the same year as Friedan’s book. Enforcement was another matter. Presidential Commission on the Status of Women status-of-women commissions status of women A federal commission created by John F. Kennedy in 1961; Eleanor Roosevelt chaired it until her death in 1962. State commissions followed. NOW was founded at their Third National Conference in 1966. Title VII Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It barred employment discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The word “sex” is in the statute. Early Equal Employment Opportunity Commission practice did not treat it as equal to race. Civil Rights Act of 1964 Civil Rights Act U.S. civil-rights statute. Title VII is the employment title. The Act is the legal floor many workplace feminists stood on; it is not itself a feminist manifesto. EEOC Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, created to enforce Title VII. NOW’s founding complaint was that the Commission was not treating sex discrimination as a real mandate. NOW National Organization for Women National Organization for Women, founded 30 June 1966 in Washington, D.C. Twenty-eight founders; Betty Friedan first president. A civil-rights-style organization for sex equality: lawsuits, lobbying, later the 1970 strike. Not the same thing as women’s liberation small groups. Pauli Murray Murray American lawyer, writer, and later Episcopal priest (1910–1985). Co-founder of NOW; co-author of its Statement of Purpose. “Jane Crow” was her name for the combined racial and sex caste she had already analyzed. Jane Crow Pauli Murray’s term for the system that constrained Black women by race and sex together — not two separate queues. Statement of Purpose NOW Statement of Purpose NOW’s 1966 founding statement. It begins by defining the organization’s purpose as bringing women into “full participation in the mainstream of American society now.” Pauli Murray helped write it. SNCC Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. A major civil-rights organization of the early 1960s. Several white women who later became women’s-liberation organizers had been trained in its discipline — and in its sex hierarchy. New Left The 1960s student and antiwar left, especially Students for a Democratic Society and related groups. A school for organizing. Also a place many women learned they were expected to type, staple, and wait. Casey Hayden Civil-rights organizer. With Mary King she wrote the 1965 memo “Sex and Caste,” circulated in SNCC, naming sex hierarchy inside the movement. Mary King Civil-rights organizer; co-author, with Casey Hayden, of the 1965 SNCC memo “Sex and Caste.” Sex and Caste Memo by Casey Hayden and Mary King, November 1965, circulated in SNCC. It compared the position of women in the movement to a caste. A document from inside civil rights, before NOW’s founding conference. consciousness-raising consciousness raising CR CR groups A women’s-liberation method: a small group speaks from its own lives, then looks for the pattern. Kathie Sarachild presented “A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising” in 1968. The point was analysis, not therapy — a distinction Carol Hanisch had to keep defending. Kathie Sarachild Sarachild New York Radical Women member. She presented “A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising” at the first national women’s-liberation conference, Chicago, November 1968. A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising Kathie Sarachild’s 1968 outline of consciousness-raising as a political method, later printed in Notes from the Second Year. New York Radical Women Early women’s-liberation group, formed in New York in 1967. Among those involved: Shulamith Firestone, Carol Hanisch, Robin Morgan, Kathie Sarachild. It organized the 1968 Miss America protest. the personal is political The Personal Is Political personal is political Phrase attached to Carol Hanisch’s 1969 memo when Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt printed it in Notes from the Second Year (1970) and gave it that title. Hanisch has said she did not name the paper. The claim: what gets called a private problem — housework, sex, abortion, shame — is a power relation. Carol Hanisch Hanisch Women’s-liberation organizer; New York Radical Women. She helped organize the 1968 Miss America protest. Her 1969 memo, titled by others in 1970, is the usual source for “the personal is political.” Notes from the Second Year 1970 women’s-liberation anthology edited by Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt. It printed Hanisch’s memo under the title “The Personal Is Political,” and Sarachild’s consciousness-raising program. Anne Koedt Koedt Feminist writer and editor. Co-editor, with Firestone, of Notes from the Second Year. Co-founder of New York Radical Feminists. Shulamith Firestone Firestone Shulie Firestone Writer and organizer (1945–2012). New York Radical Women, Redstockings, New York Radical Feminists. The Dialectic of Sex (1970). Co-editor of Notes from the Second Year. The Dialectic of Sex Shulamith Firestone’s 1970 book (William Morrow). A radical materialist argument: pregnancy and the sex class built on it are the base; cybernetic reproduction is a speculative horizon. Not a NOW pamphlet. Kate Millett Millett Writer and sculptor (1934–2017). Sexual Politics (1970), drawn from her Columbia dissertation: literature and theory as a record of patriarchy. Time put her on a cover; the fame was a trap as much as a platform. Sexual Politics Kate Millett’s 1970 book (Doubleday). Close reading of literary patriarchy — Lawrence, Miller, Mailer, Genet — as political theory. One of 1970’s two brick-sized feminist books; Firestone’s was the other. Redstockings Radical feminist group formed in New York in 1969 (Firestone and Ellen Willis among the founders). Speak-outs, including on abortion. The name plays on “bluestocking” and red. Ellen Willis Writer and critic; co-founder of Redstockings. Later a voice in the late-1970s arguments over sexuality and pornography. women’s liberation women's liberation Women’s Liberation WLM The small-group, often radical current of the late 1960s–70s, distinct from NOW’s organizational liberalism though people crossed. In Britain, Women’s Liberation Movement (WLM) is the usual name. Miss America protest Miss America No More Miss America Demonstration at the Miss America pageant, Atlantic City, 7 September 1968, organized by New York Radical Women. Freedom Trash Can on the boardwalk; a “Women’s Liberation” banner inside the hall. About two hundred people. Not a bonfire. Freedom Trash Can The barrel on the Atlantic City boardwalk, 7 September 1968, into which protesters threw bras, girdles, heels, curlers, and women’s magazines. A permit to burn the contents was denied. Robin Morgan Writer and organizer. A principal organizer of the 1968 Miss America protest; the “No More Miss America” leaflet is associated with her. Later editor of Sisterhood Is Powerful (1970). Sisterhood Is Powerful Anthology edited by Robin Morgan, 1970. A thick reader of the new movement, not a single line. Miss Black America A pageant held in Atlantic City the same night as the 1968 Miss America contest, organized as a Black alternative to a white national symbol. A different project from the boardwalk protest, on the same date. Art Buchwald American humor columnist. After the 1968 Miss America protest he helped spread the bra-burning story that the boardwalk itself had not supplied. Gloria Steinem Steinem Journalist and organizer. A public face of liberal feminism in the 1970s; a founding editor of Ms. magazine (1972). Women’s Action Alliance; National Women’s Political Caucus. Cameras could treat her as the movement. The arguments behind her were already about who “woman” included. Ms. Ms. magazine Ms magazine Feminist magazine. A preview ran in New York magazine in December 1971; the first standalone issue is 1972. Gloria Steinem was a founding editor. “Ms.” as a courtesy title was part of the point. Women’s Action Alliance Women's Action Alliance Organization co-founded in 1971 (Steinem among the founders) to supply practical feminist resources. The 12 January 1972 Leffler photograph of Steinem is from one of its news conferences. National Women’s Political Caucus NWPC National Women's Political Caucus Founded 1971 to elect women and feminist-allied candidates. Among the conveners: Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, Betty Friedan, Gloria Steinem. Bella Abzug Abzug New York congresswoman (elected 1970), lawyer, and a convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus. Later a co-chair of the National Women’s Conference in Houston, 1977. Shirley Chisholm Chisholm Brooklyn congresswoman, elected 1968 — the first Black woman in the U.S. House. She sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972. A convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus. Unbought and Unbossed (1970) is her campaign book and slogan. Unbought and Unbossed Shirley Chisholm’s 1970 book, and the slogan of her campaigns. The phrase is hers, not a later caption. Women’s Strike for Equality Women's Strike for Equality Strike for Equality Actions on 26 August 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nineteenth Amendment, called by NOW and joined by a wider coalition. A Fifth Avenue march in New York; sister actions in other cities, including Washington, D.C. Friedan had asked for a strike. What the cameras got was mostly a march. Our Bodies, Ourselves Our Bodies Ourselves Women and Their Bodies Women’s health book that began as a 1969 Boston workshop and 1970 newsprint (Women and Their Bodies) from the group later called the Boston Women’s Health Book Collective. New England Free Press, then a 1973 Simon & Schuster edition. The point was that women could know their own anatomy without waiting for a gatekeeper. Boston Women’s Health Book Collective Boston Women's Health Book Collective Boston Women’s Health Course Collective The Boston group that produced Our Bodies, Ourselves. A workshop, then a pamphlet, then a book that outlived the workshop. Title IX Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, signed 23 June 1972. “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” Sports became the public face. The text is broader. In 2002 the provision was renamed the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act. Education Amendments of 1972 Public Law 92-318, signed by Richard Nixon on 23 June 1972. Title IX is one title inside this law. Nixon’s signing statement did not dwell on the sex-discrimination provision. Patsy Mink Patsy T. Mink Mink Hawaii congresswoman. A principal House advocate of the sex-discrimination provision that became Title IX. The 2002 renaming of Title IX is after her. Birch Bayh Bayh Indiana senator. He introduced the Senate language that became Title IX, 28 February 1972. Richard Nixon Nixon U.S. president who signed the Education Amendments of 1972. The signing statement talked about higher education and busing. It did not sell Title IX as a women’s-sports law. Roe v. Wade Roe Roe v Wade U.S. Supreme Court decision, 410 U.S. 113, announced 22 January 1973. Majority opinion by Harry Blackmun, 7–2. It held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause protected a right of privacy broad enough to include a woman’s decision to terminate a pregnancy, structured in trimesters, and struck down Texas’s criminal abortion statute. It was a constitutional holding, not a statute that “legalized abortion.” Overturned in 2022 by Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization. Doe v. Bolton Companion case to Roe, decided the same day (410 U.S. 179). It struck down Georgia’s more elaborate abortion restrictions. Read with Roe, not instead of it. Harry Blackmun Blackmun Supreme Court justice; author of the majority opinion in Roe v. Wade (1973). Equal Rights Amendment ERA Proposed U.S. constitutional amendment: equality of rights shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any state on account of sex. Alice Paul introduced an ERA in 1923. Congress sent this version to the states on 22 March 1972. Original deadline 1979; extended to 30 June 1982. It fell three states short of 38. Alice Paul Suffrage organizer; author of the original Equal Rights Amendment introduced in 1923. The 1972 ERA is her text’s descendant. She belongs to the earlier capsule; the amendment did not. Phyllis Schlafly Schlafly Conservative organizer (1924–2016). STOP ERA, from 1972, argued the amendment would strip protections from housewives, send women into the draft, and attack the family. The campaign is a fact of the 1970s, not a later invention. STOP ERA Schlafly’s organization against ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment, from 1972. The stop-sign graphic is the image. The argument was that equality on paper would cost women the legal privileges of marriage and motherhood. Lavender Menace Phrase Betty Friedan used around 1969 for the fear that lesbians would discredit the movement. Reclaimed on 1 May 1970, when Radicalesbians disrupted the Second Congress to Unite Women in New York. The insult became a name. Radicalesbians Lesbian feminist group. They wrote “The Woman-Identified Woman” (1970) and staged the Lavender Menace action at the Second Congress to Unite Women, 1 May 1970. The Woman-Identified Woman Radicalesbians manifesto, 1970. It argued that lesbianism was a political position inside feminism, not a public-relations problem for NOW. lesbian feminism A current, not a single organization: the claim that intimate life with women, and a politics built from that fact, was central — not a side issue to be hidden for respectability. Combahee River Collective Combahee Black feminist lesbian socialist collective in Boston, 1974–1980. Named for the June 1863 Combahee River Raid, in which Harriet Tubman helped lead a Union expedition that freed hundreds of enslaved people. Their April 1977 statement is the text this capsule slows down for. Combahee River Collective Statement Combahee statement the 1977 statement Dated April 1977. It argues that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression are interlocking, and that Black women’s politics have to start from that fact. It uses the phrase “identity politics” for a coalition that does not require anyone to stand aside. Later printings include a 1979 anthology edited by Zillah Eisenstein. Primary authors later named: Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier. Barbara Smith Writer and organizer; co-founder of the Combahee River Collective; later of Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press. One of the three who later discussed authorship of the 1977 statement. Beverly Smith Organizer and writer; Barbara Smith’s sister; one of the three later named as primary authors of the Combahee River Collective Statement. Demita Frazier Frazier Organizer; one of the three later named as primary authors of the Combahee River Collective Statement. identity politics In the Combahee statement, a name for politics that begin from one’s own structural position — Black, woman, lesbian, working-class — without treating those as separate queues. The later pejorative use of the phrase is not the 1977 use. Black feminism A current inside the era, not a later correction pasted on. National Black Feminist Organization (1973); Combahee (1974–80); writers including the Smiths, Frazier, and, late in the window, bell hooks. The who-counts problem returning in public. National Black Feminist Organization NBFO Founded in New York in 1973 to address Black women’s position in both the women’s movement and Black politics. Combahee began among Boston women who had been in its orbit and wanted a more radical, socialist, lesbian-inclusive politics. Harriet Tubman Tubman Abolitionist. The Combahee River Collective took its name from the 1863 Combahee River Raid she helped lead. The name is a claim of descent, not a 1970s photograph of her. Combahee River Raid June 1863 Union raid on the Combahee River in South Carolina, with Harriet Tubman as a scout and leader, freeing hundreds of enslaved people. The 1970s collective borrowed the name on purpose. bell hooks hooks Gloria Jean Watkins Writer (Gloria Jean Watkins, 1952–2021). Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism (South End Press, 1981). Late in this capsule’s window: she is arguing with a movement that has already named itself, not founding NOW. She kept the name lowercase. Ain’t I a Woman Ain't I a Woman Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism bell hooks’s 1981 book. The title reaches back to Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech — and to the later refrain attached to it. In this archive that refrain’s history is in the First Wave capsule. The 1981 book is about Black women and the feminism that had trouble counting them. National Women’s Conference National Women's Conference Houston conference Houston 1977 Federally funded conference in Houston, 18–21 November 1977, following International Women’s Year. Delegates adopted a National Plan of Action (ERA, abortion, lesbian rights, minority women, and more). Three First Ladies appeared. A conservative Pro-Family rally met in Houston the same weekend. International Women’s Year International Women's Year IWY United Nations designation for 1975. It produced a Mexico City conference and, in the U.S., a commission and the 1977 Houston meeting. National Plan of Action The 26-plank document adopted at Houston in 1977, recommendations to the President and Congress. A federal-conference text. Combahee’s statement, months earlier, is a different kind of “we.” Rosalynn Carter U.S. First Lady in 1977. She appeared at the National Women’s Conference in Houston with Betty Ford and Lady Bird Johnson. Betty Ford Former U.S. First Lady; ERA supporter. On the Houston stage, November 1977. Lady Bird Johnson Ladybird Johnson Former U.S. First Lady. On the Houston stage, November 1977, with Rosalynn Carter and Betty Ford. Pro-Family rally Pro-Family Conservative gathering in Houston during the 1977 National Women’s Conference, associated with Schlafly and opponents of the ERA, abortion rights, and lesbian planks. Same city, same weekend, a different “family.” Women Against Pornography WAP Organization founded in New York in 1979. Part of the late-1970s turn toward pornography as a feminist target. The louder “sex wars” continue past this capsule’s 1982 line. MLF Mouvement de libération des femmes Mouvement de liberation des femmes Mouvement de libération des femmes. French women’s-liberation current, named in the press around a 26 August 1970 demonstration at the Arc de Triomphe. Not a branch office of NOW. Manifesto of the 343 343 Manifeste des 343 Statement published in Le Nouvel Observateur, 5 April 1971, in which 343 women declared they had had abortions, then illegal in France. Simone de Beauvoir was among the signers. Simone de Beauvoir Beauvoir de Beauvoir French philosopher. The Second Sex (1949) is earlier than this capsule. She signed the Manifesto of the 343 in 1971. A predecessor and a contemporary, depending on which book you open. The Second Sex Simone de Beauvoir’s 1949 book (Le Deuxième Sexe). A philosophical inventory of “woman” as Other. It is not a second-wave text; second-wave readers treated it as one anyway. Ruskin College Ruskin Trade-union college in Oxford. Site of the first British National Women’s Liberation Conference, 27 February–1 March 1970. Four opening demands: equal pay, equal education and opportunity, 24-hour nurseries, free contraception and abortion on demand. ūman ribu uman ribu ウーマン・リブ ribu Japanese women’s liberation of the early 1970s, from the English “women’s lib.” Tanaka Mitsu’s 1970 pamphlet Liberation from the Toilet is a founding text. Ribu Shinjuku Center (1972–77) was a shelter, clinic, and meeting place. A critique of the family system and of New Left sexism, not a translation of Friedan. Tanaka Mitsu 田中美津 Japanese ribu organizer and writer. Liberation from the Toilet (便所からの解放), 1970. A founder of the Ribu Shinjuku Center. Liberation from the Toilet 便所からの解放 Benjo kara no kaihō Tanaka Mitsu’s 1970 ribu pamphlet. It attacked the treatment of women — including by men on the left — as a receptacle. The title is hers; it is not a metaphor invented for this capsule. Ribu Shinjuku Center リブ新宿センター Ribu Sentā Women’s center and shelter in Shinjuku, Tokyo, 1972–1977. A ribu institution: housing, abortion and legal advice, a paper, a place to go. New Feminism 新女性主義 xin nüxing zhuyi Lü Hsiu-lien’s name for the feminism she promoted in 1970s Taiwan: a 8 March 1972 lecture at National Taiwan University’s law college, then the 1974 book 新女性主義. Slogans included “first a person, then a man or a woman.” This was under martial law, not under the U.S. numbering. Lü Hsiu-lien 呂秀蓮 Annette Lu Lu Hsiu-lien Taiwanese lawyer and writer (b. 1944). She introduced New Feminism in Taipei in the early 1970s after graduate study in the United States. Later vice president of the Republic of China (2000–2008). The later office is not this capsule; the 1974 book is. Stonewall Uprising at the Stonewall Inn, New York, June 1969. Gay liberation is a contemporaneous movement, not a subplot of NOW. Lesbian feminism sits in the overlap. backlash A word later attached, especially by Susan Faludi’s 1991 book Backlash, to the 1980s counter-movement: Reagan–Thatcher conservatism, anti-ERA organizing, a media story that feminism had gone too far. The word is 1991. The conservative turn is already in this lesson’s last years. Susan Faludi Faludi Journalist. Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women (1991). A later name for the 1980s, written after this capsule’s dates. Backlash Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women Susan Faludi’s 1991 book. Useful as a later diagnosis. It is not a 1977 source. Ronald Reagan Reagan U.S. president from 20 January 1981. His first term is the American half of the conservative turn this capsule ends in. Margaret Thatcher Thatcher British prime minister from 4 May 1979. The other English-speaking conservative date in the after. third wave Third Wave third-wave A later name. Rebecca Walker’s “Becoming the Third Wave” appeared in Ms. in January 1992. This lesson stops before the name. The problems the name tried to hold — race, sexuality, culture, who “we” is — were already on the table. Rebecca Walker Writer. Her 1992 Ms. essay “Becoming the Third Wave” is a usual starting citation for the phrase. It is after this capsule. Becoming the Third Wave Rebecca Walker’s essay in Ms., January 1992. A later christening, not a 1982 event. intersectionality Legal-theoretical name coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989 for the way race and sex (and other structures) compound. Combahee had already stated interlocking oppressions in 1977. The word is later. The problem is not. Kimberlé Crenshaw Crenshaw Legal scholar. “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989) is the usual origin of the word intersectionality. After this capsule; in conversation with it. Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 1989 article in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. The named origin of “intersectionality.” Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization Dobbs Dobbs v. Jackson U.S. Supreme Court decision, 2022, that overruled Roe v. Wade. Not part of the 1963–82 span. Named here only as the later fate of a 1973 holding. Levittown Postwar planned suburbs (Pennsylvania, New York, and others) associated with mass-produced houses and a racial boundary at the door. The 1958 photograph in this lesson is a house in Levittown, New York, made for House Beautiful. Architecture as a clue, not a biography of a resident. House Beautiful American shelter magazine. The Gottscho-Schleisner Levittown negatives used here were shot for it in August 1958. Nineteenth Amendment 19th Amendment U.S. constitutional amendment, ratified 1920, barring denial of the vote on account of sex. The 1970 strike chose its fiftieth anniversary. What the amendment did not undo is in the First Wave capsule. First Wave Later label for the suffrage-era public fights already treated in this archive’s Monday lesson of 16 August 2026. The who-counts problem did not end when the vote arrived. John F. Kennedy Kennedy U.S. president who created the Presidential Commission on the Status of Women in 1961. The commissions, not the Oval Office, are the useful fact here. Students for a Democratic Society SDS Major New Left student organization of the 1960s. A training ground and, for many women, a lesson in being asked to type. Chicago Women’s Liberation Union Chicago Women's Liberation Union Socialist-feminist organization founded in Chicago in 1969. Named here as one of the cities that was not New York. Second Congress to Unite Women Feminist conference in New York, 1 May 1970, where Radicalesbians staged the Lavender Menace action. Seneca Falls Village in New York State; 1848 convention site. In 1977 a torch was walked from there to Houston for the National Women’s Conference — a piece of first-wave ceremony reused as second-wave ceremony. Fourteenth Amendment 14th Amendment Ratified 1868. Roe’s majority located a right of privacy in its Due Process Clause. That reading is the 1973 holding; Dobbs rejected it in 2022. Le Nouvel Observateur French weekly. It published the Manifesto of the 343 on 5 April 1971. W. W. Norton Norton New York publisher of The Feminine Mystique in 1963. National Taiwan University NTU Taipei university. Lü Hsiu-lien lectured on New Feminism at its law college on 8 March 1972. George Washington University GWU GWU Women’s Liberation GWU Women's Liberation University in Washington, D.C. Its Women’s Liberation banner is readable in the 26 August 1970 photograph used as this capsule’s hero. LBJ Library LBJ Presidential Library Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library in Austin. The 9 November 1975 Steinem photograph was taken at a women’s conference there. Black Power Late-1960s current in Black politics emphasizing self-determination. Contemporaneous with women’s liberation; not background decoration. Fred Palumbo Palumbo New York World-Telegram & Sun staff photographer. He made the 1960 Friedan portrait in this capsule. Warren K. Leffler Leffler WKL U.S. News & World Report staff photographer. The 1970 Washington march and the 1977 Schlafly STOP ERA pictures in this capsule are his. Thomas J. O’Halloran Thomas J. O'Halloran O’Halloran O'Halloran TOH U.S. News & World Report staff photographer. The 25 January 1972 Chisholm portrait in this capsule is his. Frank Wolfe White House / LBJ Library photographer. The 9 November 1975 Steinem picture is credited to him. Gottscho-Schleisner Gottscho-Schleisner Collection Gottscho New York architectural photography firm. Their 1958 Levittown negatives, made for House Beautiful, are in the Library of Congress with no known copyright restrictions. Mrs. Robert Berman Robert Berman How the 1958 Gottscho catalog names the Levittown house in this lesson: a wife attached to a husband’s mailbox. The catalog entry is the evidence. U.S. News & World Report U.S. News & World Report collection American magazine. Staff photographs by Leffler, O’Halloran, and others, donated to the Library of Congress, are in the public domain under the deed of gift. New York World-Telegram & Sun World Telegram & Sun World-Telegram & Sun New York newspaper. Staff photographs donated to the Library of Congress, including Palumbo’s Friedan portrait, have no known restrictions. Before After suffrage, a quieter movement and a suburban ideal The First Wave (c. 1848–1920) ended, in the United States, with a constitutional sentence about the vote. What followed, in the usual textbook summary, is the doldrums: the suffrage coalition thinned, the Equal Rights Amendment that Alice Paul had already written sat in Congress, and a middle-class public story put women back in the house as if the house were a prize. The word “doldrums” is a later forecast. It describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended, and it does not mean every woman had been in that current. Suburban domesticity had an architecture. Mass-produced houses, a car in the drive, a lawn that looked like a job. Magazines sold the picture. So did advertisers and a certain kind of expert. Friedan would call the picture the feminine mystique — a destiny with appliances. The picture was never a map of the country. Black women, working-class women, and anyone who had not been offered the delicate house were already in the workplace, already in other people’s kitchens, already counted as labor. The gap the First Wave left — who counted as the “woman” the movement was picturing — did not close in 1920. It went indoors and called itself normal. Levittown, New York, 28 August 1958: the Mrs. Robert Berman house on Regent Lane, photographed for House Beautiful. The catalog files the resident as a wife of a mailbox. This is the architecture The Feminine Mystique would write against — and it was only ever one class of house. A two-story suburban house in Levittown, New York, with a car in the drive and young trees along a new lawn, 28 August 1958. There was already law at the start of the 1960s. Kennedy’s Presidential Commission on the Status of Women (1961) produced reports and a string of state commissions. The Equal Pay Act arrived in 1963. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 named sex in employment. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission then had to decide whether that word was a mandate or a joke. The school many organizers came out of was not a commission. It was civil rights and the New Left: SNCC, the antiwar movement, Students for a Democratic Society. Casey Hayden and Mary King’s 1965 memo “Sex and Caste,” circulated in SNCC, is one document of what women learned there — how to run a meeting, and who was expected to take notes in it. The era A bestseller, consciousness-raising, and laws that reached the workplace and the clinic Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique, published by W. W. Norton in 1963, is the public spark American memory keeps. It is not the cause. Friedan wrote about college-educated housewives and “the problem that has no name.” The book sold because a class of readers recognized themselves. Women who had never been offered that house did not need Friedan to tell them they were tired. Treat the book as a public starting point that magazines could review. Do not treat it as the whole movement. Betty Friedan, 1960 — three years before the book. Fred Palumbo’s World Telegram & Sun portrait is the face later attached to 1963. The useful date in the print is 1960: she is already a public person. The mystique had not yet been a bestseller. Betty Friedan in a 1960 studio portrait, three years before The Feminine Mystique.
