On 30 June 1966, at the Third National Conference of Commissions on the Status of Women in Washington, twenty-eight people founded the National Organization for Women. Friedan became president. Pauli Murray, who had already named “Jane Crow,” helped write the Statement of Purpose: women into the mainstream of American society now. NOW was built like a civil-rights organization — complaints to the EEOC, lawsuits, lobbying. It was one current. Women’s liberation small groups were another: New York Radical Women (1967), Redstockings (1969), Chicago Women’s Liberation Union, and dozens of unnamed living-room meetings. Consciousness-raising was the method. Kathie Sarachild put it on paper in 1968. You spoke from your own life until housework, sex, pay, and shame stopped looking like a private failure. Carol Hanisch wrote a memo in February 1969 defending those meetings against the charge that they were therapy. When Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt printed it in Notes from the Second Year (1970), they titled it “The Personal Is Political.” Hanisch has said the title is theirs. The claim is the era’s: the home was already a political economy. So were abortion, heterosexuality, and the unpaid second shift. How it showed: NOW, and the 26 August 1970 Women’s Strike for Equality on the Nineteenth Amendment’s fiftieth anniversary. Women’s liberation groups that would not be NOW. The Miss America protest of 7 September 1968 in Atlantic City — New York Radical Women, a Freedom Trash Can, a banner inside the hall, men kept off the action, no fire on a wooden boardwalk. The same night, a Miss Black America pageant ran in the same city as a different answer to a white national symbol. Our Bodies, Ourselves began as a 1969 Boston workshop and 1970 newsprint from the group later called the Boston Women’s Health Book Collective. Kate Millett’s Sexual Politics and Firestone’s The Dialectic of Sex both arrived in 1970. Ms. magazine’s first standalone issue is 1972; Gloria Steinem was a founding editor. Legislation, in the United States: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, signed 23 June — a sex-discrimination rule for federally funded education, with Patsy Mink in the House and Birch Bayh in the Senate; sports became the picture people could see. Roe v. Wade, 22 January 1973: a 7–2 Supreme Court, Harry Blackmun writing, held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s due-process privacy covered a woman’s decision to end a pregnancy, with a trimester framework, and struck down Texas’s criminal statute. It was a constitutional holding. It was not a law that “legalized abortion” in a sentence. Doe v. Bolton came down the same day. Gloria Steinem at the LBJ Library, 9 November 1975. The glasses and the microphone are how a movement got reduced to one person. By 1975 the arguments behind the podium — class, race, lesbianism, who “Ms.” was for — were already the story. Gloria Steinem at a lectern, long hair and aviator glasses, speaking at a women’s conference at the LBJ Library, 9 November 1975. Black feminism is inside this span, not a footnote written later. The National Black Feminist Organization formed in 1973. The Combahee River Collective, in Boston from 1974, put a statement in April 1977. Lesbian feminism had already refused to wait: Radicalesbians’ “The Woman-Identified Woman,” and the Lavender Menace action at the Second Congress to Unite Women on 1 May 1970, answering Friedan’s slur by wearing it. By the late 1970s the arguments were also about pornography and about difference — Women Against Pornography dates to 1979 — and those fights run past the 1982 line this lesson uses as a date, not as a conclusion. Shirley Chisholm announcing a run for the Democratic presidential nomination, 25 January 1972. She had been in the House since 1969. A convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus, with Steinem, Friedan, and Bella Abzug. Electoral feminism is one street. It is not the only one. Shirley Chisholm in patterned blouse and cat-eye glasses, photographed 25 January 1972 as she announced her presidential candidacy. The field A crowded field, then three things to look at closely A gallery of three portraits is the wrong picture. Name them, then stop treating the names as the era. Friedan, Steinem, Firestone, Millett. Pauli Murray at NOW’s founding. Shirley Chisholm in Congress and on a 1972 ballot. Bella Abzug. Patsy Mink and Birch Bayh on Title IX. Carol Hanisch and Kathie Sarachild on method. Robin Morgan on the boardwalk in 1968. Phyllis Schlafly on the other side of the ERA. Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier on a 1977 statement. bell hooks in 1981, late, already arguing with a “women” that had been too small. Tanaka Mitsu in Tokyo. Lü Hsiu-lien in Taipei. The Miss America action as an event that does not belong to one face. Slow down for three, as examples inside the field, not as the field. The Feminine Mystique as a public starting point. Consciousness-raising as a method. Combahee as the who-counts problem returning in public — the same problem the First Wave lesson left unfinished, under a different name. A story Friedan’s book, consciousness-raising groups, and the Combahee statement The book: Friedan gave a class of readers a plot in which their unhappiness was not a personal defect. Magazines could review that plot. Television could book it. NOW could walk through it into the EEOC’s office. The limitation is the same fact as the success. A feminism that begins with a white suburban kitchen will treat everyone else as a later chapter. Working women, Black women, lesbians — they were not later. They were already there, and the usual story did not count them well. The groups: consciousness-raising made a technique out of that omission. You did not begin with a program. You began with what had been called trivia — who does the dishes, who gets believed, who is afraid on the street — and you waited until the trivia had a structure. Hanisch’s memo is the defense of that wait. The New Left had said: those are personal problems; the revolution will fix them; type this stencil in the meantime. CR said the stencil was the revolution’s unfinished business. It could become its own trap: a room of people who already resembled each other, mistaking recognition for a census. The method does not excuse the room. It explains why the room felt like politics. The statement: the Combahee River Collective Statement, April 1977, is not an appendix to Steinem. A Black feminist lesbian socialist collective in Boston, named for Harriet Tubman’s 1863 raid, wrote that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression lock together, and that they would not be asked to choose which liberation to stand in line for. “Identity politics,” in their usage, is the opposite of a veto. It is a starting position from which coalition might be possible because no one is required to disappear. Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, and Demita Frazier are the three who later talked about writing it. The statement is the collective’s. Four years later, bell hooks’s Ain’t I a Woman (1981) is late in this window on purpose: a book arguing with a movement that had already decided what “woman” sounded like. The title borrows a nineteenth-century question this archive has already complicated. The 1981 argument is new only if you were not listening. Elsewhere Feminism in France, Britain, Japan, and Taiwan in the same years In France the press named a Mouvement de libération des femmes around a 26 August 1970 demonstration at the Arc de Triomphe. On 5 April 1971, Le Nouvel Observateur printed the Manifesto of the 343: women stating they had had abortions, Simone de Beauvoir among them. The Second Sex was already twenty years old. In Britain, the first National Women’s Liberation Conference met at Ruskin College, Oxford, 27 February–1 March 1970, and listed four demands: equal pay; equal education and opportunity; 24-hour nurseries; free contraception and abortion on demand. In Japan, ūman ribu was not a translation of a New York leaflet. Tanaka Mitsu’s Liberation from the Toilet (1970) went at the family system and at men on the left; the Ribu Shinjuku Center (1972–77) was a shelter and a clinic. In Taiwan, under martial law, Lü Hsiu-lien lectured on New Feminism at National Taiwan University on 8 March 1972 and published 新女性主義 in 1974: first a person, then a man or a woman. That is a 1970s feminism. It is not an Asian guest at an American table. The same years, in the same cities, were also civil rights, Black Power, the antiwar movement, student revolt, and, after Stonewall in 1969, gay liberation. Women’s liberation came out of those rooms and fought in them. A lesson that treated those movements as background would be repeating the error it is trying to describe. After The ERA failed in 1982, and later writers named a third wave National Women’s Conference, Houston, 19 November 1977. A White House photograph: Rosalynn Carter with Betty Ford and Lady Bird Johnson. The banner says WOMAN as if the noun were settled. A conservative Pro-Family rally met in the same city that weekend. Combahee’s statement was already six months old. Stage at the National Women’s Conference in Houston, 19 November 1977, with a WOMAN banner, a torch, and a podium marked National Women’s Conference 1977. Houston in November 1977 is one picture of a peak: a federally funded conference, a National Plan of Action, three First Ladies, a torch walked from Seneca Falls. It is also a picture of a split. The Plan included the ERA, abortion, lesbian rights, minority women. Opponents held their own rally. Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA had been at work since 1972. On 4 February 1977 her people were already at the White House fence with stop-sign stickers. Congress had sent the Equal Rights Amendment to the states in 1972. The deadline, extended, expired on 30 June 1982, three states short of thirty-eight. Phyllis Schlafly, STOP ERA, in front of the White House, 4 February 1977. The smile is part of the politics: a claim that housewives had a movement too. The ERA’s clock was already running. Phyllis Schlafly smiling, a STOP ERA badge on her coat, with other demonstrators and a White House fence behind her, 4 February 1977. Margaret Thatcher took office in May 1979. Ronald Reagan in January 1981. Susan Faludi would call the 1980s a backlash in a 1991 book of that name. The word is later. The conservative turn is in these last years: an official mood that feminism had been tried, or had gone too far, or had been a coastal taste. Roe stood until Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization in 2022. That sentence is outside the era. It belongs here as a fate, not as a twist. The turn into what gets called the third wave is a later naming. Rebecca Walker’s “Becoming the Third Wave” is 1992, in Ms. Intersectionality, as a word, is Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989. Combahee did not need the word to state interlocking oppressions. The numbered sequence — first the vote, then the rest, then a third period — is the after. It is useful until it hides the people who were never in that sequence. A question A question to keep asking When a movement says the personal is political, whose personal is allowed to count as politics? Roe v. Wade — oral argument (Oyez) Audio of the Supreme Court argument (1971) and reargument (1972), with the 22 January 1973 opinion. This is the case, not a documentary about it. Carol Hanisch — “The Personal Is Political” (1970), with the author’s 2006 note The essay as printed in Notes from the Second Year. Hanisch’s introduction is the useful correction: she did not title it; Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt did. Combahee River Collective Statement (April 1977) The 1977 text. BlackPast hosts it; the statement itself is the source. Primary authors later named: Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier. National Organization for Women — Statement of Purpose (1966) NOW’s own posting of the founding statement, co-authored in part by Pauli Murray. Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 — U.S. Department of Justice The statutory text. It is a sex-discrimination rule for federally funded education, not a sports law that later grew a statute. Education Amendments of 1972, Public Law 92-318 (86 Stat. 235) — GovInfo The enrolled law Nixon signed on 23 June 1972. Title IX is in this PDF (86 Stat. 373), not a separate act. Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 113 (1973) — Legal Information Institute The U.S. Reports text of the decision. Open transcription of the bound volume; not a summary article. Betty Friedan — The Feminine Mystique (W. W. Norton, 1963) Library of Congress catalog record. The book is still in copyright; this is the record, not a full text. Our Bodies Ourselves — the collective’s own history of the book How a 1969 Boston workshop became 1970 newsprint (Women and Their Bodies) and then the book. Institutional memory, not a scan of the first edition.

title: The bystander effect: a mechanism, then a newspaper story that was not the night
dek: What diffusion of responsibility claims, then Kitty Genovese, the Times story that launched the teaching example, and the later proof that the story was not what happened on Austin Street.
text: The bystander effect: a mechanism, then a newspaper story that was not the night What diffusion of responsibility claims, then Kitty Genovese, the Times story that launched the teaching example, and the later proof that the story was not what happened on Austin Street. 1964 (and the after of the story) This lesson starts with the concept, not the crime. Catherine “Kitty” Genovese was murdered in Kew Gardens in the early hours of 13 March 1964. The text does not describe wounds or sexual violence. It does not use a police portrait of her or of the killer. The Times story of 27 March 1964 is a primary source that later reporting — including the Times itself in 2016 — found flawed. The psychology that followed is real experimental work. The 38 silent witnesses are not. Psych / soc psych 13 Mar 1964 Kew Gardens About 3:15 a.m.: Genovese is attacked near her apartment off Austin Street. She dies on the way to hospital. 14 Mar 1964 A brief The Times runs a short item. The later front-page story has not been written yet. 27 Mar 1964 “37 Who Saw” Martin Gansberg’s front-page Times story. The headline says 37; the text says 38. None, it claims, called the police. 1968 The lab Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: group size can inhibit helping. They named the mechanism diffusion of responsibility. 2007 The correction Manning, Levine, and Collins in American Psychologist: no evidence for 38 witnesses, or that they watched, or that they all did nothing. 2016 The paper of record The Times calls its 1964 account flawed and “grossly exaggerated.” An editor’s note is later appended to the online 1964 story. Thirty-seven, or thirty-eight The Times headline of 27 March 1964 counted 37. The story under it counted 38. Reprints have used both. The slip is small and perfect: the number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed. What was stable was the moral — a city that would not pick up the phone. bystander effect Genovese syndrome The finding, from laboratory and field studies after 1964, that people are often less likely to help when others are present. Darley and Latané (1968) are the usual first citation. The effect does not require the Times’s 38 witnesses to be true. diffusion of responsibility Darley and Latané’s term: in a group, each person feels less personally responsible for acting. The more people who could help, the easier it is to assume someone else will. A mechanism tested in labs. Not a transcript of Austin Street. pluralistic ignorance A second mechanism in the helping literature: each person looks at the others, sees no one moving, and concludes the event is not an emergency. Silence reads as information. Kitty Genovese Catherine Genovese Catherine Susan Genovese Born 7 July 1935 in Brooklyn; killed 13 March 1964 in Kew Gardens, Queens, at 28. She managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and lived on Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. The person is older than the newspaper story. Kew Gardens A residential neighborhood in central Queens, around the Long Island Rail Road station and Austin Street. The murder is a Queens story that the Times turned into a story about the city. Austin Street The Kew Gardens street of the apartment and the first attack. Geography, not a set for a play. 38 witnesses thirty-eight witnesses 37 Who Saw The number the 27 March 1964 Times story made famous. The headline said 37; the body said 38. Manning, Levine, and Collins (2007) found no evidence that 38 people witnessed the murder. 37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police 37 Who Saw Murder Didn't Call the Police Martin Gansberg’s New York Times front-page story, 27 March 1964. The article that made the teaching example. The Times later judged it flawed. A. M. Rosenthal Abe Rosenthal Times metropolitan editor in 1964. He later wrote that Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy, over lunch, called the Queens killing “one for the books.” Rosenthal assigned the investigation and, the same year, published Thirty-Eight Witnesses. Martin Gansberg Times reporter whose 27 March 1964 piece carried the 37/38-witness claim and the neighbor’s line “I didn’t want to get involved.” Michael J. Murphy New York City police commissioner in 1964. In Rosenthal’s later telling, the lunch remark that started the second-day story. Thirty-Eight Witnesses Rosenthal’s 1964 book on the case. The number, bound as a title. John Darley Social psychologist. With Bibb Latané, “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility” (1968) and The Unresponsive Bystander (1970). Bibb Latané Latane Social psychologist. With John Darley, the 1968 paper and the 1970 book that built the experimental tradition textbooks still teach. Darley and Latané Darley and Latane The usual joint citation for the first bystander experiments. Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968. Group size can inhibit helping. The Unresponsive Bystander Darley and Latané, 1970. The book that named a field. The Genovese story is in the preface; the data are from the lab. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology The APA journal that published the 1968 Darley and Latané paper. Sophia Farrar A neighbor and friend who, after the second attack, went to Genovese, held her, and waited for the ambulance. The newspaper story needed her not to exist. Mary Ann Zielonko Genovese’s partner; they shared the Austin Street apartment. Part of the life the newspaper story flattened into a lesson about strangers. Winston Moseley The man convicted of the murder. This capsule names him once as a fact of the case and does not make him the subject. Robert Mozer A neighbor who shouted during the first attack; Moseley left and later returned. One of the actions the silent-38 story had to erase. Manning, Levine, and Collins Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins. American Psychologist, 2007: the 38-witness story is not supported by the archive. Rachel Manning Lead author of the 2007 American Psychologist paper that named the 38-witness story a parable. Mark Levine Co-author of the 2007 American Psychologist paper. Alan Collins Co-author of the 2007 American Psychologist paper. The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping Manning, Levine, and Collins, American Psychologist, 2007. Keep the experiments; retire the 38-witness story as history. American Psychologist APA journal. The 2007 Manning, Levine, and Collins paper appeared here. Kevin Cook Author of a 2014 history of the case; interviewed on NPR’s All Things Considered, 3 March 2014, about the police number and the interviews underneath it. Robert D. McFadden Times reporter; wrote the 4 April 2016 Winston Moseley obituary in which the paper called the 1964 account “grossly exaggerated.” Jim Rasenberger Author of “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (The New York Times, 8 February 2004), an early Times reconsideration. Kitty, 40 Years Later Rasenberger, The New York Times, 8 February 2004. Frances Cherry Psychologist who, with others, later argued that neighbors who heard a man and a woman at 3 a.m. often classified it as a private quarrel — a gendered reading the first parable did not pause for. James Solomon Director of the documentary The Witness, which records later reporters’ doubts about Gansberg’s count. The Witness James Solomon’s documentary on the Genovese case and its afterlife. A film, not a primary police file. 9-1-1 911 The U.S. centralized emergency number. In March 1964 New Yorkers reached the police by a precinct number or by dialing the operator. AT&T and the FCC announced a national 911 plan in 1968. urban apathy 1960s press name for the idea that city life makes strangers indifferent. The Genovese story was fitted to it. Ev’s Eleventh Hour The Hollis bar Genovese managed. A job, not a symbol. World’s Fair World's Fair The 1964–65 New York World’s Fair at Flushing Meadows, a few stops from Kew Gardens. Same borough, same spring, a different headline. Civil Rights Act Federal law passed in July 1964. Named here only as a same-year headline, not as a cause of the murder. The New York Times the Times The paper of the 14 March brief, the 27 March story, the 2004 reconsideration, and the 2016 judgment that the 1964 account was flawed. The concept What the bystander effect claims The bystander effect is a claim about groups, not about one Queens street. In its ordinary textbook form it says: a person is less likely to help in an emergency when other people are present. The more potential helpers, the less help. The name that stuck to the mechanism is diffusion of responsibility. Each person feels less personally on the hook. Someone else will call. Someone else is closer. Someone else already knows what this is. That is a statement about psychology. It can be true, false, or true only sometimes. It does not, by itself, require a famous murder, a number of windows, or a city that had forgotten how to be a neighbor. Those arrived later, as a story to hang the claim on. A second, related claim in the same literature is pluralistic ignorance: people treat other people’s inaction as information. If no one moves, the smoke is not a fire. If no one calls, the noise is not a crime. Silence becomes evidence. Diffusion of responsibility is about who must act. Pluralistic ignorance is about whether anything is happening. Textbooks often braid them. They are not the same sentence. The mechanism How Darley and Latané tested helping in a group John Darley and Bibb Latané designed emergencies you could run twice. A subject hears a seizure over an intercom, or sees smoke under a door, alone or with other people present — sometimes other subjects, sometimes confederates who have been told not to move. In 1968, in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, they reported “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility”: group size inhibited intervention. The 1970 book is The Unresponsive Bystander. The Genovese name is in the preface of a field. The data are from rooms where the experimenters could count. Why did they think it worked that way? Because responsibility, in their account, is not a fixed moral stock. It divides. A person alone owns the next move. A person in a group can wait, look, and assume the waiting is shared. Add the fear of doing the wrong thing in public — of being the one who overreacts — and inaction has two supports: I am not the one, and this may not be the thing. That is the theory. It is a theory about laboratories and, later, field studies. It is not yet a theory about Austin Street. Times Square, May or June 1952 — Angelo Rizzuto, Library of Congress. The 1960s press already had a story about cities as crowds. The bystander experiments gave that story a mechanism. The mechanism did not need a particular sidewalk. Pedestrians, a City Omnibus bus, and stacked billboards on a Times Square sidewalk, about 1952. The parable Kew Gardens, the Times, and the correction The teaching example came from a newspaper. Kew Gardens in 1964 was a Queens neighborhood of brick apartments, a Long Island Rail Road station, and Austin Street shops. Catherine Genovese, 28, managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and shared an apartment at 82–70 Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. There was no 911. A neighbor who wanted the police dialed a precinct or the operator. The city around them had other headlines: a World’s Fair opening in Flushing Meadows; a Civil Rights Act moving through Congress; a press already fond of the phrase urban apathy. Kew Gardens, west to east, about 1936 — Irving Underhill, Library of Congress. A generation before 1964 the neighborhood was already a grid around the railroad. The crime did not invent the place. The later story made the place stand for a whole city. Wide panoramic photograph of Kew Gardens, Long Island, looking west to east, about 1936. In the early morning of 13 March 1964 Winston Moseley attacked Genovese on the Austin Street side of the building. A neighbor, Robert Mozer, shouted; Moseley left and came back. The second attack was in a rear hallway, out of the street’s sight. Later reconstructions — Kevin Cook, the Times in 2016, the 2007 American Psychologist paper — agree on the shape: two attacks, not three; a layout that made a single continuous audience impossible. She was taken away by ambulance and died on the way to the hospital. Sophia Farrar, a neighbor, had gone to her and held her until help came. The station and the south parking lot from Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019. Genovese parked in the railroad lot, about a hundred feet from the apartment door. The cars and the signage are of this century. The cut in the ground is the same fact. Kew Gardens LIRR station and the parking lot south of the tracks, seen from Lefferts Boulevard in 2019. The Times of 14 March ran a short notice. The story that lasted was assigned two weeks later, after Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy told metropolitan editor A. M. Rosenthal, over lunch, that the Queens case was “one for the books.” Martin Gansberg’s piece of 27 March 1964 went on page one: “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police.” The text said thirty-eight. It said they had watched. It said none had called. An unidentified neighbor supplied the line the decade needed: “I didn’t want to get involved.” Rosenthal’s book the same year was Thirty-Eight Witnesses. The alley between the station and Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019 — the ground the case is attached to, in daylight, without a body. It is here as geography, not as evidence of what any window saw. A paved alley and stair from the Kew Gardens LIRR station toward Lefferts Boulevard, photographed in 2019, empty of people. Social psychology moved faster than the corrections. Darley and Latané started from the story the papers had already told. Many textbooks gave the experiments those 38 windows anyway. In 2007, in “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping,” Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins went back to the archive and wrote that there was “no evidence for the presence of 38 witnesses, or that witnesses observed the murder, or that witnesses remained inactive.” The Times, in Robert D. McFadden’s 2016 obituary of Moseley, called the 1964 account flawed and “grossly exaggerated.” Jim Rasenberger’s “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (2004) had already begun the paper’s own reconsideration. An editor’s note was later appended to the online 1964 story. After What the case still teaches — and what it taught wrongly What it taught wrongly is easy to list. There were not 38 people at 38 windows watching a single continuous crime and choosing, each of them, not to dial. Some neighbors did call. Someone went downstairs. The layout and the two attacks made a single shared audience impossible. Frances Cherry and others later argued that a woman’s voice at 3 a.m. was often classified as a private quarrel — a gendered reading the urban-apathy story did not pause for. James Solomon’s film The Witness records reporters who already doubted Gansberg’s count and did not pick the fight with Rosenthal. The number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed: the headline said 37, the story said 38. What the case still teaches is not a shrug. Some neighbors did too little. The emergency number was a maze. A press story can fit a ready moral — urban apathy, a city of strangers — and become harder to unwrite than to run. The bystander literature is larger than one street and has been tested without Gansberg’s count. The teaching problem is the one this lesson is for: a discipline can be right about a mechanism and still be wrong about the story it uses to make students care. Keep the experiments. Label the newspaper story. Do not let the correction become a second simplification — that no one failed anyone that night, or that groups never freeze a person. Diffusion of responsibility does not need 38 silent windows. It never did. A question A question to keep asking If a field’s most famous example turns out to be a newspaper story that was not the night, what should it do with the example — drop it, label it, or keep using it because the experiment still works? Martin Gansberg — “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police” (The New York Times, 27 March 1964) The article that made the teaching example. Read it as a 1964 front page, then read the 2016 correction. The Times paywall may sit in front of the archive. Robert D. McFadden — Winston Moseley obituary (The New York Times, 4 April 2016) The Times’s own later account, including the judgment that the 1964 story “grossly exaggerated the number of witnesses and what they had perceived.” Manning, Levine, and Collins — “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping” (American Psychologist, 2007) The paper that named the 38-witness story a parable. Abstract and DOI are public; the PDF may sit behind APA’s gate. Jim Rasenberger — “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (The New York Times, 8 February 2004) An early Times reconsideration, forty years on, before the 2007 journal article. NPR / All Things Considered — Kevin Cook, 3 March 2014 Cook, author of a 2014 history of the case, on the police number and the interviews underneath it. WNYC — “An Iconic Murder Helped Create the 911 System” (2014) On the emergency-number afterlife. 911 was a national project; New York’s centralized number arrives later than the murder. The piece is a radio essay, not a statute.

title: David and Goliath: how the smaller player wins
dek: Asymmetric competition, judo strategy, disruption, and differentiation — then Honda, Southwest, and Canon as cases, used only for the facts named public sources actually state.
text: David and Goliath: how the smaller player wins Asymmetric competition, judo strategy, disruption, and differentiation — then Honda, Southwest, and Canon as cases, used only for the facts named public sources actually state. frameworks, 1979–2001; cases, 1959– This is a strategy-framework lesson, not a biography of three firms and not a promise that underdogs win. Claims about Honda, Southwest, and Canon are traced to named public pieces: Harvard Business Review essays, an HBS case abstract, and a New York Times anniversary account. Operating statistics that those pages do not state are omitted. “David and Goliath” is a metaphor. It is not a dataset. Business business 1958–59 Small machines Honda Super Cub in Japan; American Honda the next year. Xerox 914: the large copier Xerox would later be slow to leave. 1963 Niceness Honda’s U.S. line: “You meet the nicest people on a Honda.” A different rider than Harley-Davidson’s. 1971 Southwest First Southwest Airlines flights in Texas: point-to-point, not a miniature major. 1979–80 Porter “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy”; then Competitive Strategy and the generic-strategy triad. 1995–96 HBR Bower and Christensen on disruptive technologies (Xerox/Canon in the list); Porter, “What Is Strategy?” (Southwest vs Continental Lite). 1999–2001 Judo Yoffie and Cusumano in HBR; Yoffie and Kwak’s book. Movement, balance, leverage — use the larger rival’s weight rather than matching it. Continental Lite copied the easy pieces In “What Is Strategy?” Porter’s warning is not that Southwest was mysterious. It is that a major could copy a fare, a smile, or a 737 and still fail, because the advantage was the fit among activities — what the major would have to stop doing. Continental Lite is his named exhibit of a partial imitation. A larger airline can borrow one piece of a smaller rival’s system and still be a larger airline with the old system attached. David and Goliath The biblical mismatch: a smaller fighter against a giant. In strategy writing it is a metaphor for asymmetric competition — not a claim that underdogs usually win. asymmetric competition Competing by a different set of activities, customers, or weapons than the incumbent, instead of matching size with size. judo strategy Judo Strategy David B. Yoffie and Mary Kwak’s name (book 2001; with Michael A. Cusumano in HBR, 1999) for using a stronger rival’s size against it: movement, balance, leverage — not a head-to-head trial of strength. David B. Yoffie Yoffie Harvard Business School professor. With Michael A. Cusumano, “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time” (HBR, January–February 1999); with Mary Kwak, the 2001 book Judo Strategy. Mary Kwak Co-author, with David B. Yoffie, of Judo Strategy (Harvard Business School Press, 2001). Michael A. Cusumano Cusumano MIT Sloan professor; with Yoffie, the 1999 HBR essay “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time.” Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time Yoffie and Cusumano, Harvard Business Review, January–February 1999. The public HBR statement of the judo metaphor: fast entrants taking on dominant incumbents without matching them blow for blow. Judo Strategy Yoffie and Kwak, Harvard Business School Press, 2001. Subtitled Turning Your Competitors’ Strength to Your Advantage. Movement, balance, leverage. disruptive innovation disruption disruptive technologies Clayton Christensen’s pattern: a simpler or cheaper offer that incumbents’ best customers do not want yet, which later moves upmarket. The 1995 HBR essay with Joseph L. Bower called these “disruptive technologies.” Clayton Christensen Christensen Harvard Business School professor. With Joseph L. Bower, “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (HBR, January–February 1995); later The Innovator’s Dilemma (1997). Joseph L. Bower Bower Harvard Business School professor; co-author with Christensen of “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave.” Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave Bower and Christensen, Harvard Business Review, January–February 1995. Why leading firms stay close to current customers and let newcomers take the offers those customers reject — including, in their list, Xerox and the small copier. The Innovator's Dilemma Christensen’s 1997 book. The classroom name that followed the 1995 essay. This capsule uses the essay, which is the public HBR source. differentiation product differentiation In Michael E. Porter’s generic strategies, competing by being different in a way buyers will pay for — not by being the same thing cheaper. In “What Is Strategy?” (HBR, 1996) he tightens this to a unique activity system and the trade-offs that protect it. Michael E. Porter Porter Michael Porter Harvard Business School professor. “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” (HBR, 1979); Competitive Strategy (1980); “What Is Strategy?” (HBR, November–December 1996). What Is Strategy? Porter, Harvard Business Review, November–December 1996. Operational effectiveness is not strategy. Strategy is a unique position, trade-offs, and fit among activities. Southwest Airlines is one of his exhibits; Continental Lite is the failed copy. How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy Porter, Harvard Business Review, March–April 1979. The five-forces essay: rivalry, entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers. Competitive Strategy Porter’s 1980 book. The three generic strategies — cost leadership, differentiation, focus — live here. The 1996 essay is the later, tighter public statement this capsule leans on. generic strategies Porter’s 1980 triad: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. A map of positions, not a promise that any one of them wins. Honda Honda Motor American Honda Honda Motor Company. In the U.S. motorcycle market it did not first beat Harley-Davidson at large bikes. It sold small, everyday machines to people who had not been Harley’s customer. Soichiro Honda Co-founder of Honda Motor. The NYT’s 2009 anniversary piece is the public named source this capsule uses for the U.S. entry story. Harley-Davidson Harley The incumbent American motorcycle name: large bikes, a heavyweight identity. The larger rival in the Honda story — strong in a market Honda first declined to contest head-on. Super Cub Honda 50 Honda Super Cub Honda’s small step-through motorcycle (1958 in Japan; sold in the U.S. as a small Honda, sometimes the Honda 50). The machine of a different customer. You meet the nicest people on a Honda Honda’s U.S. advertising line, from 1963. The NYT’s 2009 account calls the approach attacking “with niceness”: a different rider than the existing American motorcycle identity. Honda (A) Harvard Business School case (product 384049, 1983) on Honda’s history and U.S. entry, drawing on an earlier case and the Boston Consulting Group’s motorcycle work. Public abstract on the HBR store page; the full case is paid. Boston Consulting Group BCG Consulting firm. Its 1975 report Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry became the planned-strategy version of Honda’s rise — the version Richard Pascale later argued with. Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry Boston Consulting Group report, 1975, for the British government. The planned, scale-curve telling of Honda that classrooms used before Pascale’s interviews. Richard Pascale Author of “Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda’s Success” (California Management Review, 1984). The Honda Effect: much of what worked in America was improvised after the large bikes failed. Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda's Success Pascale, California Management Review, 1984. Interviews with Honda executives that complicate the BCG story of a deliberate small-bike plan. Honda Effect Classroom name for the fight between a planned Honda (BCG) and an emergent Honda (Pascale). A warning against treating a later success as a strategy that was clear on day one. Southwest Airlines Southwest U.S. airline that, from 1971, flew point-to-point on one aircraft type instead of copying the majors’ hub-and-spoke machine. Porter’s 1996 HBR essay uses it as a system of activities; Continental Lite is the copy that did not fit. Herb Kelleher Cofounder and longtime CEO of Southwest Airlines. Bill Taylor’s HBR remembrance (8 January 2019) is the named public source this capsule uses for the person. The Legacy of Herb Kelleher, Cofounder of Southwest Airlines Bill Taylor, Harvard Business Review, 8 January 2019. A remembrance, not a case exhibit — used here for the person, not for invented operating numbers. Bill Taylor Cofounder of Fast Company; author of the 2019 HBR piece on Kelleher. point-to-point Flying city to city without forcing a connection through a hub. Southwest’s network idea; the opposite of the majors’ hub-and-spoke. hub-and-spoke The major-airline network: feed traffic through a few hub cities. Efficient for a large system; slow and expensive to copy if you are small and want the plane back in the air. Boeing 737 The aircraft type Southwest standardized on. One type means one training school, one spare-parts list, one way to turn a plane. Porter’s point is the fit, not the airframe as a fetish. Continental Lite Continental Airlines’ 1990s attempt to copy pieces of Southwest. Porter’s 1996 essay uses it as the exhibit of a failed partial imitation: a few activities, not the system. Xerox The incumbent of large, often leased, office copiers after the Xerox 914 (1959). Bower and Christensen’s 1995 HBR essay: Xerox let Canon create the small-copier market. Xerox 914 Xerox’s 1959 plain-paper copier. The machine that made copying a corporate center, and that made a later small copier look, to Xerox’s best customers, like a toy. Canon Japanese camera and later copier company. In Bower and Christensen’s 1995 list, the firm that created the small-copier market while Xerox stayed with the customers who wanted big machines. incumbent The firm already strong in a market. Strength here is also a constraint: the customers, assets, and habits that make a new offer look small or wrong. For Honda in America, 50 Years of Going Its Own Direction New York Times, 12 July 2009. Named anniversary account of American Honda’s U.S. entry: Pico Boulevard, small motorcycles, Harley and the British bikes as the existing taste, “niceness” as the attack. Rita McGrath Columbia strategy professor. Later commentary has used Southwest as a caution about treating a famous case as a finished recipe. Named here as a limit, not as a source for 1971 facts. Grey Advertising The agency associated with Honda’s U.S. “nicest people” campaign. Named as the usual advertising credit; this capsule does not invent the internal memo. Netscape The 1990s browser company in Yoffie and Cusumano’s 1999 HBR examples of a fast entrant meeting a giant. Microsoft The incumbent in that 1999 HBR pairing. An example from their moment, not a third case in this capsule. Harvard Business Review HBR The journal that published the Porter, Christensen/Bower, and Yoffie/Cusumano essays this capsule cites. A magazine, not a method. California Management Review The journal that published Pascale’s 1984 Honda interviews. The other file in the Honda Effect. The New York Times New York Times NYT Publisher of the 12 July 2009 Honda anniversary account used as a named public source. The problem Why matching a larger rival head-on usually fails A smaller player who attacks an incumbent where the incumbent is already strong is usually volunteering to lose. The larger firm has the customers, the dealers, the plant, the brand, and the lawyers. Matching it blow for blow is a trial of strength. Judo, in the martial-art sense Yoffie and Kwak borrow, is the opposite idea: do not oppose strength to strength. Use the other side’s size against it. That is the problem this lesson is for. Not “how to be inspiring.” Not a tour of three beloved companies. The question is narrower: when the other side is larger, where do you stand so that their size becomes slow? The painting is the metaphor, not the evidence. Strategy frameworks exist because the Bible is not a market study. Caravaggio’s David with the head of Goliath. The framework Three strategy tools, each from a named essay Three named tools, from named essays, because a Saturday business lesson that invents a framework is just a slogan. Judo strategy, as David B. Yoffie and Michael A. Cusumano put it in “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1999), is how a fast entrant takes on a dominant incumbent without a sumo match. The 2001 book with Mary Kwak spells the principles as movement, balance, and leverage: define a space the larger firm is slow to enter, refuse a tit-for-tat that favors its size, and turn its assets — dealers, legacy product, current customers — into things it cannot abandon quickly. The HBR essay’s examples are of their internet moment (Netscape and Microsoft, among others). The pattern is older than the browser. Disruptive technologies, in Joseph L. Bower and Clayton Christensen’s “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (HBR, January–February 1995), are offers that today’s best customers reject. Leading firms, the essay says, invest aggressively in what those customers already want. They are late to what looks worse on the old scorecard. Bower and Christensen’s list is blunt: “Xerox let Canon create the small-copier market.” The later classroom word is disruption. The 1995 mechanism is the one this lesson uses: the incumbent is strong, therefore slow, because the wrong customers are speaking. Differentiation, in Michael E. Porter’s Competitive Strategy (1980), is one of three generic strategies: be different in a way buyers will pay for, rather than only cheaper. The tighter public statement is “What Is Strategy?” (HBR, November–December 1996). Operational effectiveness is not strategy. Strategy is a unique position, the trade-offs that come from choosing what not to do, and fit among activities. Porter’s Southwest Airlines is not a mood. It is a system. His Continental Lite is what happens when a larger airline copies a few pieces and keeps the rest of the old machine. Product differentiation is one weapon inside that system — a different customer, a different product, a different activity set — not a logo exercise. Read the three together and the pattern is one sentence: do not attack the place the larger firm is already strongest; attack the thing it cannot leave without becoming a different company. Porter’s 1979 essay “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” is the prior question — what industry are you even standing in — before you pick a fight. The cases Three company cases, used only for the facts the sources state Honda versus Harley-Davidson is the small-bike case. The New York Times’s 12 July 2009 anniversary piece, “For Honda in America, 50 Years of Going Its Own Direction,” puts American Honda on Pico Boulevard in 1959, facing a market whose available machines were Harley-Davidsons or British bikes. Honda’s larger models did not do the job those riders already had. The Super Cub — the small Honda, the Honda 50 in American speech — did a different job for a different person. The 1963 line “You meet the nicest people on a Honda” is the public face of that choice. The Times calls it attacking with niceness. In framework language: movement into a space Harley’s identity made expensive to enter, and a product differentiated by who was allowed to look normal on it. The Honda story is also a warning about hindsight. The HBS case Honda (A) (384049, 1983) tells the U.S. rise in part through the Boston Consulting Group’s Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry (1975) — a planned, scale-curve Honda. Richard Pascale’s “Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda’s Success” (California Management Review, 1984) is the other file: executives who said they had no strategy beyond seeing whether they could sell something, large bikes that failed on American roads, Super Cubs used as staff transport until strangers asked where to buy them. The Honda Effect is the name of that argument. Use the case. Do not pretend the slide was written in 1959. A first-generation Honda Super Cub. The point is the scale of the machine, not a sales chart. Harley’s strength was a different motorcycle and a different rider. Caption the object; do not invent the volume. A first-generation Honda Super Cub, step-through frame, small engine, 1958 design. Southwest versus the U.S. majors is the activity-system case. First flights in 1971, Texas, Herb Kelleher among the founders. The public abstract of Vijay Govindarajan and Julie Lang’s Southwest Airlines case states the skeleton this lesson is allowed to use: short-haul, point-to-point, a cost structure the majors did not have. Porter’s 1996 essay is the framework reading: one aircraft type, the Boeing 737; a network that did not worship hub-and-spoke; trade-offs a full-service major could not make without wrecking the rest of its system. Bill Taylor’s 2019 HBR remembrance, “The Legacy of Herb Kelleher, Cofounder of Southwest Airlines,” is for the person, not for a turnaround-minute that this lesson will not invent. Continental Lite, in Porter, is the larger airline that picked up a few of the pieces and kept the old system on. A Southwest Boeing 737–700, photographed later than 1971. The airframe family is the point Porter needs: one type, one way to turn the plane. The livery is of this century. The idea is not. A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737–700 in canyon-blue livery, landing. Canon versus Xerox is the disruption case already named in Bower and Christensen. The Xerox 914 had made large, often leased, plain-paper copying a corporate center. Those customers wanted more of that. A small copier looked like a worse 914. Canon (and, in the wider history, other Japanese firms) made the small machine for offices that did not have a copy center. Xerox’s strength — the installed base, the service revenue, the definition of a serious copier — was the reason to wait. The 1995 essay’s sentence is the claim: Xerox let Canon create the small-copier market. This lesson does not add a unit count the essay does not give. Limits What the pattern does not explain Judo does not mean the small player is wiser. Sometimes the larger firm is right, and the new offer stays a toy. Christensen’s pattern is famous enough to be over-applied: not every cheaper product is a disruptive technology, and not every incumbent who ignores a niche is about to die. Porter’s fit can become a prison; the same activity system that Continental Lite could not copy can, later, be a reason not to change when the industry does. Rita McGrath and others have since used Southwest itself as a caution about treating a case as eternal. That later argument is not this lesson’s exhibit. It is a reminder that a framework is a lens, not a prophecy. Honda’s two files — BCG and Pascale — are the honest ending. A smaller player can win by attacking where the incumbent is strong and therefore slow. A smaller player can also win because a large bike broke, a clerk asked about the cub, and someone at Grey Advertising wrote a line about nice people. Strategy writing after the fact is very good at turning the second story into the first. The job is to keep both stories in view. After The companies changed; the advice is still about not copying a larger rival’s strengths The 1999 HBR judo essay was written for internet time. The 1995 disruption essay was written for disk drives and copiers and excavators. Porter’s 1996 Southwest is a system that later managers have been tempted to unpick. The pattern — do not fight the larger firm where it is already strongest — is what remains worth teaching on a Saturday. The companies are evidence. They are not saints. A question A question to keep asking If the incumbent’s strength is also the reason it cannot move, what would count as evidence that you are the smaller player with a real opening — and not just the next Continental Lite? David B. Yoffie and Michael A. Cusumano — “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1999) The public HBR statement of judo strategy. Paywall possible; the title and the claim are on the open page. Joseph L. Bower and Clayton M. Christensen — “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1995) Why incumbents stay with current customers. The open summary names the Xerox/Canon line this capsule uses. Michael E. Porter — “What Is Strategy?” (Harvard Business Review, November–December 1996) Position, trade-offs, fit. Southwest is an exhibit; Continental Lite is the failed copy. Michael E. Porter — “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” (Harvard Business Review, March–April 1979) The five-forces essay. Industry structure before you pick a fight with a Goliath. Honda (A) — Harvard Business School case 384049 (1983) Public abstract: Honda’s history and U.S. entry, drawing on an earlier case and BCG’s motorcycle work. Full text is paid. “For Honda in America, 50 Years of Going Its Own Direction” (The New York Times, 12 July 2009) Named anniversary account: Pico Boulevard, small bikes, Harley and the British machines as the existing taste. Bill Taylor — “The Legacy of Herb Kelleher, Cofounder of Southwest Airlines” (Harvard Business Review, 8 January 2019) A remembrance of Kelleher. Used for the person, not for fleet counts. Vijay Govindarajan and Julie Lang — “Southwest Airlines” (Tuck / HBS-linked case abstract) Public abstract: short-haul, point-to-point, lowest-cost structure in the domestic industry. Not a license to invent turnaround minutes.
