title: War of Resistance (1937–45): the war that did not wait for 1939
dek: From the clash at the Marco Polo Bridge to the wartime capital in Chongqing, this is a world war looked at from China, not as Asia’s footnote to Europe.
text: War of Resistance (1937–45): the war that did not wait for 1939 From the clash at the Marco Polo Bridge to the wartime capital in Chongqing, this is a world war looked at from China, not as Asia’s footnote to Europe. 1937–1945 This lesson looks out from China. Europe’s 1939 is contemporaneous, not the frame. “World War II” as a 1939–45 European story leaves 1937–39 as a preface. From Chongqing, 1939 is the year the European war caught up. Nanjing is treated with one careful image of a city after bombing — no corpses as illustration. Casualty figures that cannot be sourced here are omitted. History history 1931–32 Mukden / Lytton Japan seized Manchuria after the Mukden Incident. The League of Nations sent the Lytton Commission. The full-scale war was still ahead. 1937 Lugou / Shanghai 7 July at the Marco Polo Bridge; the Battle of Shanghai opened in August and made the war visible to foreign cameras. 1937 Nanjing The capital fell in December. Massacre followed. This lesson will not decorate that fact with bodies. 1938–43 Chongqing Wartime capital after the retreat up the Yangtze. Years of bombing. People lived in tunnels. 1939 Europe Germany invaded Poland. A second opening of a world war, not the first. 1945 Surrender / after Japan surrendered. The Chinese civil war did not wait long. Memory became a second fight between states. Europeans named the bridge for a traveler The stone bridge at Wanping is 盧溝橋, the Lugou Bridge. Europeans called it the Marco Polo Bridge because Polo’s Travels describe a fine bridge in this region. The 1937 incident entered English under the traveler’s name. The soldiers at Wanping were not fighting over a memoir. They were fighting over a crossing and a railway town. The nickname is a European label that stuck. War of Resistance 抗日戰爭 Second Sino-Japanese War Chinese name for the full-scale war with Japan, conventionally dated from 7 July 1937 to 1945. Some Chinese histories include 1931. This capsule uses 1937–45 as the full-scale span and treats 1931 as the before. Marco Polo Bridge Lugou Bridge 盧溝橋 Lugouqiao Stone bridge over the Yongding River near Wanping, southwest of Beiping. A clash beginning 7 July 1937 became the opening of full-scale war. Europeans had long called it the Marco Polo Bridge. Wanping 宛平 Walled town at the north end of the Lugou Bridge. The 1937 incident is a fight over a railway town and a crossing, not a symbol. United Front Second United Front The uneasy wartime cooperation between the Nationalists (KMT) and the Communists after 1937, following the Xi’an Incident of 1936. A front is not a friendship. It is an agreement about who the enemy is this year. Chongqing Chungking 重慶 Sichuan city that became the Nationalist wartime capital after the fall of Nanjing and the retreat up the Yangtze. Japanese bombing of the city, 1938–43, is one of the long air campaigns of the war. Battle of Shanghai August–November 1937. Urban fighting that made the war visible to foreign concessions and foreign cameras. It did not save Nanjing. Nanjing Massacre Nanking Massacre Rape of Nanking After the city fell in December 1937, Japanese troops killed civilians and disarmed soldiers on a mass scale and committed widespread rape. This capsule names the event and does not illustrate it with bodies. Lytton Commission League of Nations commission, 1931–32, led by Lord Lytton, sent to investigate Japan’s seizure of Manchuria after the Mukden Incident. Its report rejected Japan’s account. Japan left the League. The war of 1937 still came. Mukden Incident 18 September 九一八 18 September 1931: an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway used by the Kwantung Army as a pretext to seize Mukden (Shenyang) and then Manchuria. The before of 1937. National Revolutionary Army NRA The Nationalist government’s army, commanded in this war by Chiang Kai-shek. Not the only Chinese armed force in the field; the Communists fought as well, under the United Front’s strained roof. Xi’an Incident December 1936: Zhang Xueliang detained Chiang Kai-shek in Xi’an to force a turn from civil war toward resistance against Japan. The Second United Front follows. A kidnapping used as policy. Beiping Peking Beijing The city now called Beijing. In 1937 it was Beiping — “Northern Peace” — because the Nationalist capital was Nanjing. Names in this capsule follow the political geography of the year. Before Japan had already seized Manchuria in 1931 On 18 September 1931 the Kwantung Army used an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway as a pretext to seize Mukden (Shenyang) and then Manchuria. The League of Nations sent the Lytton Commission. The commissioners walked tracks, took testimony, and produced a report that did not accept Japan’s story. Japan left the League. The occupation stayed. Investigators on a Manchurian railway — the kind of scene the Lytton Commission’s 1931–32 inquiry produced. A League report can name a pretext. It could not put the province back. Men in suits and hats inspecting a railway track in an open landscape. Inside China the 1930s were also a civil war. The Xi’an Incident of December 1936 — Zhang Xueliang detaining Chiang Kai-shek — forced a turn: a Second United Front against Japan. The front was a cease-fire with a shared enemy, not a merger of the Nationalists and the Communists. That is the politics standing behind 7 July 1937. The era The 1937 fighting spread from Wanping to Shanghai, Nanjing, and Chongqing On the night of 7 July 1937 a Japanese unit near the Lugou Bridge claimed a missing soldier and demanded entry to Wanping. Shots followed. The incident did not stay local. By the end of the month Beiping and Tianjin were gone. In August the Battle of Shanghai opened a war that foreign concessions could photograph from their own rooftops. The fighting lasted into November. It did not save Nanjing. Chiang Kai-shek, in the field, looking through binoculars — a wartime command image. The Nationalist state would lose its capital and move the government upriver. The man in the cap is not the whole war. He is the government that had to relocate. Chiang Kai-shek in uniform looking through binoculars, other officers behind him. A civilian pulling a household — chairs, boards, a rocking horse — through a city street. The War of Resistance is a military history. It is also this: millions of people walking inland with what a cart would hold. A man pulling a cart piled with furniture and a child’s rocking horse through a Chinese city street. Nanjing, the capital, fell in December 1937. What followed is the Nanjing Massacre: mass killing of civilians and prisoners, mass rape. This lesson uses one photograph of a city after air attack — rubble, people standing in it, no bodies arranged for the lens. The event does not need a corpse to be believed. If you need numbers, go to the historians who argue over them in public. They are not invented here. A Chinese city after bombing, 1937 — the archive filename places it in Nanjing. People in the frame are standing. This is the one Nanjing image in the lesson: a capital made into a field of rubble, not a gallery of the dead. Civilians standing in a wide field of rubble after the bombing of a Chinese city, 1937. The government went to Chongqing. From 1938 the city was bombed, again and again, for years. People lived in tunnels. The wartime capital is not a footnote to the fall of France. It is where the Republic of China was still a state. A Japanese bomber over a river city, smoke on the ground — the archive identifies the campaign against Chongqing. From the air, a capital is a target set. From the ground, it is a schedule of sirens. A Japanese twin-engine bomber over a river city, smoke plumes on the ground. In September 1939 Germany invaded Poland. From London that is when “the war” begins. From Chongqing it is the year the European war joined a war already two years old. The United Front still held, badly. Zhou Enlai in the Nationalist capital was diplomacy as much as alliance. Xiao Hong, who had already fled the Northeast, died in 1942 in Japanese-occupied Hong Kong — a writer’s war, not a general’s. Zhou Enlai (center) with the American journalist Edgar Snow and Deng Yingchao, 1938. The United Front had to be explained to foreigners as well as fought. A photograph of three people standing is not a merger of two parties. Zhou Enlai in a dark suit standing between Edgar Snow and Deng Yingchao. People A general, a diplomat, a writer Chiang Kai-shek 蔣介石 1887–1975 Head of the Nationalist government and commander of the National Revolutionary Army. He lost the coast and kept a state in Sichuan. The after of 1945 — civil war, then Taiwan — is also his. Wartime command photograph, looking through binoculars. Zhou Enlai 周恩來 1898–1976 Communist representative in the United Front’s public face. Chongqing and the liaison work are part of how the Chinese Communist Party survived the war as a political fact, not only as a guerrilla force. 1938, with Edgar Snow and Deng Yingchao. Xiao Hong 蕭紅 1911–1942 Born in the Northeast. The Field of Life and Death and a short life lived as a refugee — Wuhan, Chongqing, Hong Kong. She died in 1942. A war of resistance is also a war of people who were not in uniform. Xiao Hong, a 1930s portrait. A story What a refugee cart was carrying In the Shanghai refugee photograph the cart is a household turned into a load. The rocking horse is the detail that makes the load a family. This is not a cute war. It is a reminder that “home front” in this war often meant there was no front that stayed put, and home was something you carried. Europe in 1939 produced its own carts. That does not make 1937 a rehearsal. After Japan surrendered in 1945, and the Chinese civil war resumed Japan surrendered in August 1945. The United Front did not become a peace. The civil war resumed; by 1949 the People’s Republic was proclaimed in Beijing and the Republic of China’s government was on Taiwan. Memory split with the states. In the PRC the War of Resistance is a founding story. In Taiwan it is also a founding story, with different heroes. In Japan the same years are a different argument still. If a later Friday lesson takes 1945–49, it will not be to tidy this one. It will be because the after is a war of its own. A question A question to keep asking If a world war is dated from 1939, whose 1937 was demoted to a preface? The Battle of China (1944) — Why We Fight U.S. Army orientation film, Frank Capra series. Public-domain American wartime framing of the China theater — useful as a primary object, not as a neutral history. Internet Archive.

subject: literature
title: High modernism (c. 1910–30): writers break the ordinary sentence
dek: Woolf, Joyce, and Eliot changed how a novel or a poem could move through time. In the same years, the magazine 新青年 and Lu Xun changed the written language of Chinese literature. They are contemporaneous events, not a required pairing.
text: High modernism (c. 1910–30): writers break the ordinary sentence Woolf, Joyce, and Eliot changed how a novel or a poem could move through time. In the same years, the magazine 新青年 and Lu Xun changed the written language of Chinese literature. They are contemporaneous events, not a required pairing. c. 1910–30 “High modernism” is a later classroom name for a cluster of European and American experiments with form, especially in the 1910s–20s. The people in this lesson did not agree they were in a school. This lesson looks out from London, Paris, and Dublin — the usual triangle — and then notices that 1918 in Shanghai is the same year, not a sidebar assigned to make the triangle look global. Literature literature 1914 Blast The Vorticist magazine appeared in London. Then the First World War arrived, which the magazine’s type had been rehearsing as noise. 1916 Portrait Joyce’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man appeared in book form. 1918 狂人日記 / 新青年 Lu Xun’s “A Madman’s Diary” was printed in New Youth, vol. 4, no. 5. Vernacular Chinese became a literary event. 1919 May Fourth Student protests in Beijing against the Versailles settlement’s handling of Shandong. A political date that literary history also has to hold. 1922 Ulysses / Waste Land Joyce published Ulysses in Paris through Shakespeare and Company; Eliot published The Waste Land in London. A year the syllabus never lets go. 1925–27 Woolf Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse. A day, a house, and a mind used as structure instead of a plot summary. The Waste Land came with notes attached When Eliot published The Waste Land in book form in 1922, he added notes. Some explain quotations; some are jokes; some have been treated as a key to a locked poem. He later said the notes began as a way to pad a slim book. Whether you believe the shrug or not, the notes are part of how the poem was sold and taught. A modernist fragment can arrive with its own apparatus. high modernism High modernism modernism Later critical name for early-twentieth-century formal experiment — fragmentation, interiority, mythic scaffolding — especially in English-language literature around 1910–30. The writers did not vote for the label. stream of consciousness A way of writing a mind in motion: associations, sensory fragments, not always a tidy paragraph. Woolf and Joyce are the usual English-language exhibits. The phrase is a critic’s tool, not a 1922 brand name. Ulysses Joyce’s 1922 novel, published in Paris by Shakespeare and Company. One day in Dublin (16 June 1904), a Homeric scaffolding, and a censorship history in the English-speaking world. The Waste Land Waste Land Eliot’s 1922 poem. Fragments, quotations, notes. Ezra Pound cut it. The notes are part of the poem’s public life, not a teacher’s appendix only. Mrs Dalloway Woolf’s 1925 novel. A day in London, a party, a war still in the body of a man who was in it. Time is the structure. Blast Short-lived Vorticist magazine, London, 1914–15, edited by Wyndham Lewis, with Pound among the contributors. Two issues. The cover is a manifesto in type. 新青年 New Youth La Jeunesse Xin Qingnian Chinese magazine, founded 1915 by Chen Duxiu (first as 青年雜誌 / Youth Magazine). The May 1918 issue printed Lu Xun’s “A Madman’s Diary.” It argued for vernacular writing and a new culture in the same years Europe was calling itself modern. May Fourth 五四 May Fourth Movement 4 May 1919: student protests in Beijing against the Versailles settlement’s handling of Shandong. “May Fourth” also names a wider New Culture moment — language, gender, science, the nation — that is not a footnote to London. 狂人日記 A Madman’s Diary Diary of a Madman Lu Xun story, 1918, written in vernacular Chinese. A reader who sees cannibalism in the classical tradition. It is a modernist event in a different language politics. Shakespeare and Company Sylvia Beach’s Paris bookshop. It published Ulysses in 1922 when British and American houses would not. A shop can be a press. Bloomsbury Loose London circle (Woolfs, Bells, Keynes, Strachey, and others). Useful as an address. Misleading if you use it as a synonym for all of modernism. Vorticism London avant-garde around Lewis and Blast, briefly, just before and into the First World War. A British answer to Futurism that did not last as a movement and left a very loud magazine. vernacular Chinese 白話 baihua Written Chinese closer to speech, as opposed to classical literary Chinese. The New Culture argument was that literature had to change language, not only subject. Lu Xun’s 1918 story is a landmark in that change. Before Nineteenth-century narrative still walked the reader through time The novel and the poem, in the late nineteenth century, could still pretend that time moved in a straight sequence. Even when they doubted that, they usually guided the reader from one event to the next. The decade before 1914 was already restless — free verse, impressionism, a city speeding up — but the First World War is the fact that later readers use to explain why that sequence broke. It is not the only fact. Cities, psychoanalysis, new print, and a reading public that included more women and more students were already changing who literature was for, and how it could be written. Virginia Stephen, photographed by George Charles Beresford in 1902 — years before Mrs Dalloway. The public-domain portrait is of a young woman who had not yet written the books this lesson is about. That is useful. Modernism did not arrive fully formed in a 1922 jacket. Virginia Woolf in profile, 1902, photograph by George Charles Beresford. The era The usual syllabus clusters around 1922; Shanghai had 1918 From London and Paris the syllabus bunches around 1922: Ulysses from Sylvia Beach’s shop; The Waste Land in The Criterion and then as a book, cut by Ezra Pound. Woolf’s major novels come a few years later, but the method is in the same family — a day, a mind, a city, and a refusal to narrate as if a life were a plot summary. Stream of consciousness is the critic’s name for that method. The writers were trying to put on the page how attention actually moves: associations, sensory fragments, not always a tidy paragraph. James Joyce, photographed by C. P. Curran in 1918, while Ulysses was still appearing in parts and still unfinished. The book would be a 1922 Paris object. The face is already the one the century kept. Sepia portrait of James Joyce with glasses and a goatee, around 1918. T. S. Eliot as a young man in a study — the usual furniture of the poet as intellectual. The Waste Land (1922) is not only a study poem. It is a collage of other people’s lines, a London of the war’s aftermath, and a set of notes that became part of the work’s public life. T. S. Eliot as a young man in a study, holding a pipe. The same years, not as a required pairing: in Shanghai, 新青年 (New Youth / La Jeunesse) was arguing that Chinese literature had to change its language. The May 1918 issue printed Lu Xun’s 「狂人日記」. A reader in that story sees cannibalism in the classical tradition. In 1919, May Fourth made the language argument a street protest as well as a magazine fight. This is not “the Asian Woolf.” It is a contemporaneous fight about vernacular writing, the nation, and who a written sentence is for — happening while Eliot was assembling fragments and Joyce was finishing a day in Dublin. 新青年 4:5, May 1918. The contents list includes 魯迅’s 「狂人日記」. The French title La Jeunesse is on the cover. A Shanghai magazine, in the same decade as Blast and Ulysses, announcing that the language of literature would have to change. Cover of New Youth magazine, volume 4 number 5, May 1918, listing 狂人日記 by 魯迅. Lu Xun, Shanghai, 24 September 1930, inscribed at age fifty. The photograph is later than “A Madman’s Diary.” It is the face that the 1918 story, and the years after May Fourth, made public. Studio portrait of Lu Xun in a light changshan, dated Shanghai, 24 September 1930. Blast, in 1914, is the London version of a public manifesto. Two issues, then a war that killed some of the people who might have kept the magazine going. High modernism is often taught as quiet interior monologue. The pink cover is a reminder that it also wanted to be a poster. People Four writers, one decade, not one school Virginia Woolf 1882–1941 Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927), A Room of One’s Own (1929). She used the sentence as a record of attention: what a mind notices in a day, not a plot summary of a life. Bloomsbury is the address, not the whole explanation. Beresford’s 1902 portrait, years before the novels. James Joyce 1882–1941 Dublin on the page, published in Paris when London and New York houses were still afraid of the book. Ulysses is one day (16 June 1904), a Homeric scaffolding, and a censorship history. Shakespeare and Company was a bookshop that became a press. Curran’s 1918 photograph, while the book was still unfinished. T. S. Eliot 1888–1965 American-born, London-settled. The Waste Land is the poem the century assigned to 1922. The notes, the quotations, and Pound’s cuts are part of the object, not extras a teacher added later. A study portrait from the early career. Lu Xun 魯迅 1881–1936 Zhou Shuren. “A Madman’s Diary,” then a body of stories, essays, and translations that made vernacular literary Chinese a fact. He is in this lesson because 1918 is 1918 — not because a Western syllabus needed an Asian twin. Shanghai, 1930, later than the 1918 story. A story Two magazines, one decade, two different projects Blast 1, 1914. The word is the picture: a title used as a poster. Blast magazine cover, 1914. Put Blast next to 新青年. One is a London roar in English, two issues, then a war. The other is a Shanghai magazine that ran for years and printed a story that helped change the written language. They are not the same project. They share a decade in which people decided the old sentence was part of the problem. That is enough of a reason to put them in one lesson. It is not a reason to make one the key to the other. After How these books became a teaching canon By the 1930s the experiments had become a canon in some places and a target in others. Woolf died in 1941; Joyce the same year; Lu Xun in 1936; Eliot lived long enough to become a monument. The after of high modernism is partly a teaching machine: 1922 as a fetish year, stream of consciousness as a worksheet. The after is also every later writer who inherited the broken narrative sequence and had to decide whether to restore it. If this archive later takes a Thursday to a different literature, it will not be to complete a set. It will be because another year also happened. A question A question to keep asking When a syllabus says “1922,” whose 1918 was dropped to make the year look clean? T. S. Eliot reads The Waste Land (recording) The text is 1922. Recordings circulate legally via libraries and the Poetry Foundation’s page; this is not a film of 1922. James Joyce reads from Finnegans Wake (Anna Livia Plurabelle) Internet Archive copy of Joyce’s own recording. Later than Ulysses; still his voice.

subject: film
title: French New Wave (c. 1958–64): the camera leaves the studio
dek: Young French critics attacked the polished studio cinema they called the tradition of quality, then made their own films in real streets with lighter cameras. A 1959–62 burst of features, and a magazine that had already trained an audience, gave the press a name: Nouvelle Vague.
text: French New Wave (c. 1958–64): the camera leaves the studio Young French critics attacked the polished studio cinema they called the tradition of quality, then made their own films in real streets with lighter cameras. A 1959–62 burst of features, and a magazine that had already trained an audience, gave the press a name: Nouvelle Vague. c. 1958–64 “Nouvelle Vague” was a press label before it was a school. The people in this lesson argued in Cahiers du Cinéma, learned at the Cinémathèque as much as at the official film school IDHEC, then made films that did not look like the tradition de qualité they had been attacking. This lesson looks out from Paris. Free Cinema, the Japanese New Wave, and cinéma vérité were happening in the same years. They are not assigned peers. Taiwan New Cinema is a later relative that borrowed the “new cinema” idea, not a 1960 contemporary. Film film 1951–54 Cahiers Cahiers du Cinéma was founded in 1951. Truffaut’s 1954 essay “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” named the tradition de qualité as the enemy. 1955–58 Before the name Varda’s La Pointe Courte and Chabrol’s Le Beau Serge. Critics were already picking up cameras before the press had a label for them. 1959 Cannes Les Quatre Cents Coups and Hiroshima mon amour. The festival gave international journalists a date they could print. 1960–62 The burst À bout de souffle, Paris nous appartient, Lola, Jules et Jim, and Cléo de 5 à 7 arrived in a short stretch of years. 1960s Elsewhere Free Cinema and the British New Wave; the Japanese New Wave; cinéma vérité. Same years, different arguments with their own studios. 1980s A later relative Taiwan New Cinema. The French name traveled. Travel is not the same as origin. The jump cuts were also a way to shorten the film Godard and editor Cécile Decugis shortened Breathless by cutting inside shots, not only between them. The jump cut is now taught as a philosophy of time. It was also a way to lose running time without reshooting Paris. Both things can be true: a device can be an idea and a solution to a reel that was too long. Nouvelle Vague New Wave French New Wave Press name, late 1950s, for a cluster of mostly young French directors who had often been critics first. A useful label, and a bad census of everyone who was making films that way. tradition de qualité tradition of quality Tradition of Quality cinéma de qualité Truffaut’s hostile name for the polished, literary, studio-bound French cinema of the 1940s–50s that Cahiers wanted to replace. “Quality” here is an insult. ciné-clubs ciné-club Postwar French film societies that screened and argued over films outside the commercial circuit. A training ground before a camera was a job. IDHEC The official French film school (Institut des hautes études cinématographiques). The New Wave’s joke was that you could learn more in the dark at the Cinémathèque than in its classrooms. Cinémathèque Cinémathèque française The Cinémathèque française, the archive and screening room associated with Henri Langlois. For the Cahiers critics it was a school: Hollywood and Europe, night after night. Henri Langlois Co-founder of the Cinémathèque française. The programmers’ programmer: he showed the films the school and the industry had filed as disposable. André Bazin Critic and co-founder of Cahiers du Cinéma. A father figure the younger writers both used and argued with. Cahiers du Cinéma Cahiers French film magazine, founded 1951. Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, and Rohmer wrote there. The magazine trained an audience and then supplied directors. politique des auteurs auteur theory Cahiers argument: a director can be the author of a film the way a novelist is the author of a book — including in Hollywood, if the films have a signature. In English this hardened into “auteur theory.” It was a polemic, not a law of nature. auteur The director-as-author, in the Cahiers sense. A fighting word before it was a festival brochure word. Alfred Hitchcock Hitchcock Hollywood director the Cahiers critics treated as an author, not a genre mechanic. The insult to French “quality” was the point. Howard Hawks Hawks Hollywood director claimed by Cahiers as an auteur. Hawks, Hitchcock, Nicholas Ray: the American names in the French fight. Nicholas Ray Hollywood director (Rebel Without a Cause and others) whom Cahiers treated as a signature, not a studio employee. jump cut jump cuts An edit that skips a bit of time inside a continuous shot, so the image jerks. Breathless made the device famous as style, not as a mistake to be hidden. Cameflex Éclair Cameflex Eclair Cameflex Lightweight French 35mm camera (Éclair). New Wave crews used cameras like this because they could leave the studio. available light Shooting with the light already in the street or room, rather than a studio grid. An aesthetic with a budget attached. location shooting Filming in real streets and rooms instead of sets. Italian neorealism had already done this; Paris made it look like a choice and a generation. Left Bank Later grouping of filmmakers including Varda, Resnais, and Marker — often more essayistic than the Cahiers men. Useful as a map, and too neat if you treat it as a wall. Georges de Beauregard Producer of Breathless and other early New Wave features. The movement had a checkbook, not only a manifesto. Pierre Braunberger Producer who backed several New Wave and Left Bank films. Another name for the fact that cheap was not free. François Truffaut Truffaut Critic, then director. “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” (1954); Les Quatre Cents Coups (1959). The man who attacked the tradition of quality later became, himself, a kind of tradition. Jean-Luc Godard Godard Critic, then director. À bout de souffle (1960) is the film people mean when they say “jump cut.” The longer fact is a director who treated cinema as an argument. Claude Chabrol Chabrol Cahiers critic, then director. Le Beau Serge (1958) is often called the first New Wave feature — a provincial story, not a Paris postcard. Jacques Rivette Rivette Cahiers critic, then director. Paris nous appartient (1961) is a Paris of plots and rooms, longer-breathed than the jump-cut cliché. Éric Rohmer Eric Rohmer Rohmer Cahiers critic and later editor, then director of talkative moral tales. In the 1959–62 burst he is already in the magazine’s inner room. Agnès Varda Agnes Varda Varda Photographer first, then filmmaker. La Pointe Courte (1955) is often called a New Wave film before the name. Cléo de 5 à 7 (1962) is the later public proof she was not a guest. Alain Resnais Resnais Left Bank director. Hiroshima mon amour (1959) is a literary, time-tangled film from the same Cannes season as The 400 Blows — not a Cahiers boys’ night out. Chris Marker Marker Essay-filmmaker of the Left Bank. A name on the map even when a given year’s famous titles are someone else’s. Jacques Demy Demy Director of Lola (1961). A musical intelligence in the same years; often parked beside Varda, which is geography and a marriage, not a full account. Louis Malle Malle Director of Les Amants (1958). Adjacent to the burst: a scandal about adult desire, not a Cahiers calling card. Jean-Pierre Léaud Léaud Actor; Antoine Doinel in Les Quatre Cents Coups and later Truffaut films. A new face who became a recurring one. Jean Seberg Seberg American actress; the American in Paris in À bout de souffle. Breathless without her face is a different object. Jean-Paul Belmondo Belmondo Actor; the petty criminal in À bout de souffle. A new star who looked like he had walked in from the street. Anna Karina Karina Actress and Godard’s collaborator in the films just after Breathless. A face the New Wave kept walking back to. Raoul Coutard Cinematographer of Breathless, Jules et Jim, and many other New Wave films. Handheld, available light, a camera that could walk. Cécile Decugis Cecile Decugis Editor of Breathless. The jump cuts are hers as well as Godard’s. Marguerite Duras Novelist and screenwriter of Hiroshima mon amour. The literary half of a film the Cahiers story likes to file under directors only. Antoine Doinel The boy in Les Quatre Cents Coups, played by Jean-Pierre Léaud. Truffaut returned to him. A character, not a mascot. Une certaine tendance du cinéma français Truffaut’s 1954 Cahiers essay attacking the tradition of quality. A fight about scripts, adaptation, and who authors a film. Le Beau Serge Chabrol, 1958. Often cited as the first New Wave feature: a return to a provincial town, shot away from the studio comfort the essay had mocked. Les Quatre Cents Coups The 400 Blows 400 Blows Truffaut, 1959. Cannes made it an international event. Antoine Doinel in a Paris that is not a postcard. À bout de souffle Breathless A bout de souffle Godard, 1960. Jump cuts, handheld, a thin crime plot. The event is the grammar. Cléo de 5 à 7 Cléo from 5 to 7 Cleo de 5 a 7 Cléo Varda, 1962. A singer walks through two real-time hours of Paris while she waits for a medical result. Hiroshima mon amour Resnais, 1959, screenplay by Duras. A French actress and a Japanese man; time that will not stay in order. Cannes, the same season as The 400 Blows. Jules et Jim Truffaut, 1962. A triangle, a stretch of the century, a camera that keeps moving. The film that made the New Wave look like it could also be tender and long. Paris nous appartient Paris Belongs to Us Rivette, 1961. Conspiracy and rehearsal in a city that will not explain itself. Lola Demy, 1961. Nantes, a dancer, a musical pulse without yet being a full musical. Often parked beside Varda, which is geography and a marriage, not a full account of the film. Les Amants Malle, 1958. A bourgeois adultery film that became a censorship fight. Next to the New Wave, not inside its magazine. La Pointe Courte Varda, 1955. A fishing village and a marriage, often called a New Wave film before the name existed. Free Cinema British mid-1950s documentary movement (Anderson, Reisz, Richardson and others): short films, everyday subjects, a manifesto. Contemporaneous, not a French export. Edward Yang Taiwan New Cinema director. Again: 1980s, a cousin, not a contemporary. François Truffaut’s 1954 Cahiers du Cinéma essay “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” is the fight in print. The other half of the fight was the politique des auteurs. A director, even in Hollywood, could be an author. Alfred Hitchcock counted. So did Howard Hawks. So did Nicholas Ray. The insult to the French studio system was the point: if those American directors were authors, the polished French adapters were not. They had learned the argument in rooms that were not IDHEC, the official French film school. Postwar ciné-clubs trained an audience to argue. The Cinémathèque française, under Henri Langlois, showed Hollywood and Europe as if the distinction did not matter. André Bazin’s Cahiers, founded in 1951, hired the arguers: Truffaut, Jean-Luc Godard, Claude Chabrol, Jacques Rivette, Éric Rohmer. The official school existed. The joke — and it was only half a joke — was that you learned more in Langlois’s dark than in a curriculum. What was new in Paris was the combination: critics who became directors, a magazine that had already trained an audience, faster film stock, lighter cameras, and producers — Georges de Beauregard, Pierre Braunberger — willing to bet on a low budget that looked like a choice. The era What the films looked like once they left the studio The look is easy to list and easy to turn into a costume. Location shooting. Jump cuts. Available light. Young non-stars or new faces: Jean-Pierre Léaud, Jean Seberg, Jean-Paul Belmondo, Anna Karina. Handheld cameras, Raoul Coutard walking them through traffic. A 1959–62 burst in which it suddenly seemed that everyone who had written for Cahiers, and several people who had not, had a feature. Left Bank versus the Cahiers group is a map of that burst, not a ranking: Varda, Alain Resnais, Chris Marker, Jacques Demy on one side of a useful line; Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, Rohmer on the other. Louis Malle’s Les Amants (1958) sits beside that cluster. The line leaks. That is why it is a map and not a membership list. The Latin Quarter as a working street, not a back lot. New Wave location shooting made Paris look like a place people already lived — which is why the city in these films still feels like itself, and why a production still needed permits, light, and luck. Rivette’s Paris nous appartient (1961) makes the city a rumor of plots and rehearsals. Demy’s Lola (1961) finds a musical pulse in Nantes. The press needed a date anyway. Cannes, 1959, supplied one. The field Many filmmakers, and three films to look at closely Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, Rohmer, Varda, Resnais, Marker, Demy, Malle: that is already too many for a poster and too few for a census. Add the actors — Léaud, Seberg, Belmondo, Karina — and the people who made the images possible: Coutard, Cécile Decugis, Duras, Beauregard, Braunberger, Langlois, Bazin. Deepen only a few works, as examples inside the field. Les Quatre Cents Coups is the public breakthrough. Truffaut, who had been banned from Cannes as a critic, arrived in 1959 as a director and won best director. The film follows Antoine Doinel, played by Jean-Pierre Léaud, through a Paris that is not a postcard — school, streets, a runaway, a freeze-frame on a beach. It is the date the press needed. It is not the first film in the cluster. It is the one that made the cluster visible abroad. À bout de souffle is the film that made the jump cut famous as a choice, not a mistake. Godard, 1960; Belmondo and Seberg; Coutard’s camera; Decugis in the cutting room. The plot is a thin crime story. Time skips inside shots. The hero talks as if the audience were in the room. Later classrooms will call this a philosophy. It was also a way to shorten a film without reshooting Paris. Both things can be true. Cléo de 5 à 7 and Hiroshima mon amour keep the map from collapsing into two men and a jump cut. Varda’s 1962 film walks a singer through two real-time hours of Paris while she waits for a medical result. Resnais’s 1959 film, from a Duras screenplay, refuses to let time stay put: a French actress, a Japanese man, a city that is not Paris. La Pointe Courte had already been Varda’s earlier claim, in 1955. If “auteur” only fits the Cahiers men, the word is too small. Agnès Varda (left), early 1960s. The filename on this archive print says Venice, 1962 — the year of Cléo de 5 à 7. Treat the place-name as the archive’s label. The person is not in doubt: a director who was already working when the magazine men picked up cameras. Agnès Varda, short dark hair, standing with another woman on a wooden deck over water. A later photograph of a portable camera on a tripod. This is not a 1959 production still. It is here because the New Wave’s bet — that a lighter camera changes who gets to shoot, and where — did not stay in Paris. The equipment traveled. The date of this picture is later than the era. The idea is the era’s. Children looking through a professional motion-picture camera on a tripod, with an adult nearby. Elsewhere The same years, different arguments In Britain, Free Cinema’s shorts and manifesto — Lindsay Anderson, Karel Reisz, Tony Richardson — had already argued for everyday subjects and a camera that did not owe the studio a polished lie. The British New Wave features that followed are contemporaneous, not a French franchise. In Japan, Nagisa Oshima, Shohei Imamura, Hiroshi Teshigahara and others were breaking studio form; the phrase nūberu bāgu borrows the French name and then goes its own way. Cinéma vérité — Jean Rouch and Edgar Morin’s Chronicle of a Summer (1961) — is another French argument of the same years: not fiction’s jump cut, but a claim on the present tense. These are contemporaneous arguments, not a ranking with France at the top. After Later filmmakers borrowed the methods, and a later cinema borrowed the name American studios in the late 1960s needed a younger audience and had lost the old Production Code’s certainty. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the sentence film histories use to connect Paris to New Hollywood. The connection is real and incomplete. A lot of other things — television, the draft, the collapse of the studio system’s weekly habit — were part of the same American turn. Taiwan New Cinema, in the 1980s — Hou Hsiao-hsien, Edward Yang, and others — is sometimes filed as another “new wave.” It is a later relative: a different state, a different language politics, a different argument with its own studios. It does not belong on the 1958–64 timeline except as a reminder that the French name traveled, and that travel is not the same as origin. title: British Invasion (c. 1963–67): Britain sells America its own records back
dek: After rationing, British teenagers learned guitar from American R&B and rock and roll 45s. Skiffle, art schools, and pirate radio turned those records into a local scene. In 1964 American radio named the export a “British Invasion.”
text: British Invasion (c. 1963–67): Britain sells America its own records back After rationing, British teenagers learned guitar from American R&B and rock and roll 45s. Skiffle, art schools, and pirate radio turned those records into a local scene. In 1964 American radio named the export a “British Invasion.” c. 1963–67 “British Invasion” is an American radio and press name for British beat groups hitting the U.S. charts after February 1964. From Britain the same years were also the end of rationing’s long after-effect, a BBC that still limited how many records it could play, pirate radio ships, and a generation that had learned guitar from American R&B and rock and roll records. This lesson looks out from Britain. Motown, the Beach Boys, French yé-yé, and Japanese Group Sounds were running in the same years. They are not decoration, and they are not a required Asia pairing. Music music 1954–56 After rationing Meat rationing ended in 1954. Lonnie Donegan’s “Rock Island Line” (1955–56) made skiffle a cheap way for teenagers to start a group. 1962 Labels / managers Decca passed on the Beatles; Parlophone and George Martin did not. Brian Epstein was already managing them. London R&B clubs were covering Chess and Motown records. 1964 Sullivan / Caroline The Beatles appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show on 9 February. Radio Caroline began broadcasting from a ship in March. The American name “British Invasion” arrived with those months. 1964 London riff The Kinks released “You Really Got Me.” The Rolling Stones kept their Chicago R&B sources louder than variety television preferred. 1965–66 Elsewhere Motown and Stax were hit factories in the United States. The Beach Boys were in the studio. Group Sounds bands were working in Japan. Yé-yé was already on French radio. 1967 The name shrinks Sgt. Pepper, BBC Radio 1, and the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act. Psychedelia made “Invasion” too small a word for what the records were doing. The BBC was limited in how many records it could play Into the mid-1960s the BBC was bound by needle-time: agreements with the Musicians’ Union that limited how many hours of records, as opposed to live studio bands, could be broadcast. Pirate ships were not only a teenage romance. They were a way around a labor and licensing rule. Radio 1, created in 1967, was in part an official answer to that gap. British Invasion American press and radio name, from 1964, for the rush of British beat groups onto the U.S. charts. The people in Liverpool and London did not need the phrase to know they were already playing. skiffle British 1950s homemade jazz-folk-blues: acoustic guitar, washboard, tea-chest bass. Lonnie Donegan’s hit version of “Rock Island Line” (1955–56) put a cheap guitar in a lot of teenage hands. needle-time needle time BBC agreements with the Musicians’ Union that limited how many hours of records (as opposed to live studio bands) could be broadcast. Pirate ships were one way around the rule. R&B rhythm and blues In early-1960s Britain, “R&B” usually meant Black American rhythm and blues and Chicago electric blues — Chess Records, Motown, the records imported or covered in London clubs — not the later pop-chart sense of the letters. rock and roll rock & roll The 1950s American form British teenagers heard on imported 45s and the few U.S. package tours that reached them. Berry, Little Richard, and the rest were a curriculum before they were a nostalgia act. pirate radio Unlicensed stations on ships or forts outside British territorial waters, from 1964. They played the records the BBC’s Light Programme would not schedule in bulk. Radio Caroline The first major British pirate pop station. It began broadcasting in March 1964 from a ship in international waters. Merseybeat The early-1960s Liverpool beat-group sound and scene, named for the River Mersey. The Beatles were the export; they were not the only band in the city. Mod Mods A British youth style of the early-to-mid 1960s: sharp Italian tailoring, scooters, R&B and soul records, later associated with the London look that Carnaby Street sold. A look and a market, not a single band. Carnaby Street Carnaby A short Soho street that became a 1960s boutique strip. The British groups traveled as clothes as well as singles. beat groups beat group The British name for the guitar-bass-drums-vocals groups that filled cellars and ballrooms before “British Invasion” was an American headline. package tours package tour British multi-act road bills: several groups, one night, a shared bus. How most of the country met the records between television appearances. art schools art school British art colleges that a striking number of 1960s musicians passed through. They were cheap, they taught looking, and they left time to form a group. Chess Chess Records Chicago label (Phil and Leonard Chess) that recorded Chuck Berry, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf. British groups learned the catalog; American radio had often filed it as R&B, not pop. Motown Detroit label founded by Berry Gordy. By 1964 it was a hit factory with its own sound, choreography, and crossover ambition — running in the same years as the Invasion, not waiting to be discovered by it. Stax Memphis label and studio whose house band and singers made Southern soul in the mid-1960s. Another American industry, contemporaneous, not a British invention. Group Sounds グループ・サウンズ Japanese 1960s electric-guitar pop, mid-decade: The Tigers, The Spiders, The Blue Comets. It heard the Beatles and local kayōkyoku at once. Same years, different market. yé-yé French and wider European mid-1960s pop named for the “yeah-yeah” refrain. France Gall, Sylvie Vartan, and others were already on the radio while Britain was invading America. kayōkyoku Japanese popular song of the postwar decades, the domestic tradition Group Sounds bands were hearing alongside imported beat records. Vox AC30 AC30 British 30-watt guitar amplifier, from the late 1950s. The Beatles, the Shadows, and later Invasion groups used it. The chime is a hardware fact, not a metaphor. Ed Sullivan The Ed Sullivan Show Sunday-night U.S. television variety show. The Beatles’ 9 February 1964 appearance is the Invasion’s most repeated American date. It was a broadcast, not the beginning of the music. Parlophone EMI label that signed the Beatles in 1962, with George Martin as producer. Not a small indie — a wing of a large British record company that had room for comedy records and, it turned out, beat groups. Decca British label that, in January 1962, did not sign the Beatles after an audition. It later had the Rolling Stones. A large company can be late and still be in the business. EMI The British record group that owned Parlophone. The Invasion’s “independent” look sat on major-label machinery. BBC Light Programme The British public broadcaster. In the early 1960s its Light Programme carried pop, but needle-time limited how many records it could play. Radio 1, in 1967, was in part an official answer to the pirates. Radio 1 BBC pop network launched in 1967, after the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act squeezed the pirates. An official station for a habit the ships had already trained. Lonnie Donegan Scottish-born skiffle singer. “Rock Island Line” (1955–56) showed a British teenager that an American folk-blues song could be a hit without an orchestra. Lead Belly Leadbelly American folk-blues singer (Huddie Ledbetter). Donegan’s “Rock Island Line” came from his repertoire. Rock Island Line American folk-blues song. The Animals Animals Newcastle group with an R&B repertoire, later filed under the Invasion in America. The city is not London; the set list still came from American records. Dave Clark Five the Dave Clark Five DC5 Tottenham group. American television used them as the next British name after the Beatles. A beat group from north London, not Merseybeat. Dusty Springfield British pop and soul singer. She is in the Invasion years and not a beat group: a reminder that the American name flattened more than guitars. Manfred Mann London R&B and pop group (and the keyboardist they were named for). Another name on the 1964–65 bills. The Hollies Hollies Manchester group. The Invasion was not only Liverpool and London. The Yardbirds Yardbirds London R&B group. A club band that made the guitar a problem to be solved, not only a riff to be copied. The Shadows Shadows British instrumental group of the late 1950s–60s. The Vox AC30 was already a local sound before the Invasion name existed. Berry Gordy Founder of Motown. In 1964 his label was not waiting to be invaded. The Temptations Temptations Motown group. “My Girl” is 1964: a parallel American industry, not a footnote to Sullivan. My Girl Temptations / Motown single, 1964. Same year as the Sullivan appearance. The Beach Boys Beach Boys California group. Contemporaneous with the later Invasion years; not caused by them. France Gall French yé-yé singer, already a radio name in the mid-1960s. Sylvie Vartan French yé-yé singer. Before After rationing, cheap guitars, and other people’s records Postwar Britain did not jump from the Blitz to Carnaby Street. Food rationing lasted into the 1950s; meat came off the ration in 1954. What followed was not sudden luxury. It was a narrower fact: a generation that had more pocket money than its parents at the same age, and not enough official culture that sounded as if it belonged to them. The BBC’s Light Programme carried pop. It did not carry enough of it. Needle-time agreements limited recorded music on air. If you wanted more than the official dose, you needed a radio that was not polite, a shop that imported American 45s, or — later — a ship that was not yet in British waters. The records arrived first. Rhythm and blues and rock and roll came as merchant-seamen singles, as classified imports, and as the B-sides of things the Light Programme did not love. Chuck Berry’s “Johnny B. Goode” was a 1958 Chess single from Chicago. Little Richard, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf, and the Motown 45s were the rest of the homework. Manchester had the Hollies. Newcastle had the Animals. Tottenham had the Dave Clark Five. None of this required an American name yet. It required halls, managers, and a BBC that still could not play the records as often as the rooms wanted them. The era How a local scene became an American headline What Americans later called the British Invasion was, from Britain, several overlapping facts. Beat groups filled ballrooms and package tours. Merseybeat and London R&B were not the same accent: Liverpool sold harmony and a smile that television could use; London’s R&B clubs sold Chess covers and longer hair. The look traveled with the singles. Mods, Italian suits, scooters, then Carnaby Street as a boutique strip a tourist could photograph. Teen papers — New Musical Express, Melody Maker, and the American fan magazines that followed — treated the groups as a weekly serial. The industry underneath was not a cottage. Parlophone, Decca, EMI, managers such as Brian Epstein and Andrew Loog Oldham, and producers such as George Martin were large companies and a few intermediaries who had learned that a cellar residency could be a product. The field Many groups, and three ways they entered the story A gallery of three faces is the wrong picture. The field is crowded on purpose. The Beatles, the Rolling Stones, the Kinks, the Who, the Animals, the Dave Clark Five, Dusty Springfield, Manfred Mann, the Hollies, the Yardbirds — and behind them the American records they learned: Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Motown, Chess. Epstein and Oldham sold the dates. Martin, and the Decca that said no, are the industry’s two hands. Donegan is the cheap starter kit. Sullivan is the American camera. Liverpool, Hamburg, the Cavern Club, then Parlophone. This lesson does not need another press shot of four men in suits. The useful facts are the repertoire and the timing. They had already learned Berry, Little Richard, and the girl-group records. “I Want to Hold Your Hand” was a song American radio could not file as a foreign novelty for long. After Sullivan, every other British group on an American bill was using an introduction they had not made. That is not the same as saying the others were copies. It is a fact about cameras and charts. The Rolling Stones are the R&B debt left audible. London clubs, Chess covers, Jagger and Richards, and Oldham’s refusal to package them as variety. They did not invent Muddy Waters. They declined, longer than was polite, to pretend the covers were a phase. When they wrote their own songs, the debt was still the point: a British group selling America a Chicago idea with white faces on the same variety shows that had not booked the Chess roster as pop. The honest version does not scold them for learning. It keeps the Chess label in the shot. Treat the hardware story as the usual one; the record is the fact. Liverpool’s export was blend. This was a two-chord shove from Muswell Hill. It is one record, not a theory of the decade. It is enough to stop the Invasion from being told as four smiling men and one television broadcast. Elsewhere The same years, not a ranking of songs In Detroit, Motown under Berry Gordy was already a finished system — writers, a house band, a finishing school for movement. The Temptations’ “My Girl” is 1964. In Memphis, Stax was cutting Southern soul with a biracial house band. In California the Beach Boys were in the studio; Pet Sounds, in 1966, is the comparison the syllabuses never let go. In France, yé-yé — France Gall, Sylvie Vartan — was already a word. In Japan, Group Sounds bands (the Tigers, the Spiders, the Blue Comets) were taking electric guitars into a market that had its own kayōkyoku tradition. Britain was not the only place the 45 rpm single was rewriting a generation. It was the place American television decided to point the camera. That is a fact about power, not a ranking of songs. After By 1967 the chart label no longer described the music By 1966–67 the useful Invasion story — verse, chorus, suit, scream — was already too small. Revolver, then Sgt. Pepper, then a lot of other people’s sitars and tape loops. The turn toward psychedelia was not a British monopoly; San Francisco is in the same late decade. The name “British Invasion” stays useful as a 1964–65 American chart event. It is a poor name for everything that happened next. The Marine Broadcasting Offences Act arrived in 1967. Radio 1 began the same year. The pirates were legislated against. The records did not disappear from British life. A question A question to keep asking If a country sells another country its own music, who counts as the inventor in the room? The Beatles on The Ed Sullivan Show (9 February 1964) Sullivan’s own site on the broadcast. Full performances are licensed; this is the historical record of the date, not a bootleg film. Chuck Berry — Johnny B. Goode (1958) Chess single 1691. The record many British groups learned from. Official/label upload; if it moves, search the title on the label’s channel. The Beatles — I Want to Hold Your Hand (1963) The Capitol single that opened the U.S. market in late 1963 and early 1964. Official Beatles channel. The Kinks — You Really Got Me (1964) Official audio. Distorted riff, London, not Liverpool. The Temptations — My Girl (1964) Motown, same year as the Sullivan appearance. Not a footnote — a parallel industry. Radio Caroline The station still exists. The 1964 ship is history; the site is the living remnant, not a 1964 tape.

subject: feminism
title: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): the fight over whether women counted as political persons
dek: From Seneca Falls to the Nineteenth Amendment, women in the United States and Britain organized for the vote and for legal standing. The movement split over race, tactics, and who was included when organizers said “we.”
text: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): the fight over whether women counted as political persons From Seneca Falls to the Nineteenth Amendment, women in the United States and Britain organized for the vote and for legal standing. The movement split over race, tactics, and who was included when organizers said “we.” c. 1848–1920 “First wave” is a later Anglo-American classroom name. The people in this lesson did not call themselves that. The label is useful because it groups several decades of public campaigns over whether women counted as political persons. It is incomplete as a history, because those campaigns were not only Anglo-American, and because they did not include every woman they claimed to speak for. What follows uses the usual dates, then looks at the same years in China. Feminism feminism 1848 Seneca Falls A two-day convention in Seneca Falls, New York, issued the Declaration of Sentiments. The vote was one demand among many legal and social grievances. 1851 Akron Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from a later rewrite of that speech. 1870 The split The Fifteenth Amendment barred denying the vote because of race, not sex. Stanton and Anthony opposed ratifying it without women; Stone and Douglass would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait. 1907 Anqing Qiu Jin was executed after an uprising in Anqing. She was working in the same decade as British militant suffragettes, under a different government. 1913 Procession / Derby On 3 March, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized a suffrage procession in Washington, D.C. In June, Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby. 1920 Nineteenth Amendment The United States barred denying the vote because of sex. Poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence still blocked many Black women in the South. She copyrighted her own photograph In 1864 Sojourner Truth registered the copyright on her own cartes-de-visite in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan. That was unusual: the photographer usually claimed the image. The cards were printed with her own sentence, “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” She sold them at lectures because lectures did not pay enough. The portrait in this lesson is one of those cards. The “shadow” here is her word for the photograph, not a later flourish. coverture English common-law doctrine that a married woman’s legal identity was “covered” by her husband’s. Property, contracts, and wages were his unless a statute carved out an exception. separate spheres A nineteenth-century middle-class rule: men belonged in public and economic life, and women belonged in the home as moral guardians. It was a class rule as much as a sex rule. Women who earned wages, and enslaved women, were never offered that protected private role. Seneca Falls Village in western New York. On 19–20 July 1848 a convention there issued the Declaration of Sentiments. Later writers used “Seneca Falls” as shorthand for the start of organized U.S. women’s rights. It is a useful date, not the only origin. Declaration of Sentiments Sentiments The 1848 Seneca Falls text, modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It listed grievances including the vote. The vote was not the only demand, and not everyone in the room wanted it named first. Fifteenth Amendment 15th Amendment Ratified 1870. It barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. The omission split the U.S. women’s-rights coalition. WSPU Women’s Social and Political Union Women’s Social and Political Union, founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst. The militant wing of British suffrage: window-breaking, hunger strikes, and, in reply, force-feeding. Jim Crow The system of legal racial segregation and disenfranchisement in the U.S. South after Reconstruction — poll taxes, literacy tests, violence. The Nineteenth Amendment did not repeal it. 中國女報 Chinese Women’s Journal Chinese Women’s Journal, edited by Qiu Jin in Shanghai in 1907. Two issues appeared. It argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same breath as anti-Qing politics. carte-de-visite cartes-de-visite A small albumen photograph mounted on card, cheap to reproduce, sold and collected in the 1860s. Sojourner Truth sold hers with a printed caption and a copyright in her own name. Gage Frances Dana Gage Frances Dana Gage. In 1863 she published a version of Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech that includes the refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. Nineteenth Amendment 19th Amendment Ratified 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not touch poll taxes, literacy tests, or the violence that still blocked many Black women in the South. force-feeding In British prisons, hunger-striking suffragettes were restrained and fed through a tube. The Liberal government presented it as medical care. Militants presented it as assault. Both descriptions circulated in the press. doldrums A later name for organized U.S. feminism in the 1920s–1950s. After the vote arrived, the suffrage coalition thinned and public campaigning quieted. The word describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the underlying questions ended. Alice Paul American suffrage organizer. She trained with British militants, then with Lucy Burns planned the 3 March 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington. She later led the National Woman’s Party and wrote an Equal Rights Amendment. Married Women’s Property Acts Married Women's Property Acts Married Women’s Property Act State statutes, beginning in the 1840s, that let a married woman keep some property in her own name. New York’s 1848 act is the usual example. The laws were limited and uneven. They did not end coverture. National Woman Suffrage Association NWSA Founded in 1869 by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony after the split over the Fifteenth Amendment. It opposed ratifying the amendment without women and worked for a federal suffrage amendment. American Woman Suffrage Association AWSA Founded in 1869 by Lucy Stone and others who would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait for women. It favored a state-by-state strategy. It merged with the NWSA in 1890. National American Woman Suffrage Association NAWSA The 1890 merger of the National Woman Suffrage Association and the American Woman Suffrage Association. The main constitutional-suffrage organization in the United States until the Nineteenth Amendment. Cat and Mouse Act Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Act Prisoners Temporary Discharge for Ill Health Act British 1913 statute that released hunger-striking suffragettes when they were too weak to feed, then rearrested them when they recovered. The nickname compared the government to a cat playing with a mouse. Xu Xilin 徐錫麟 Hsü Hsi-lin Anti-Qing revolutionary. His 1907 uprising in Anqing failed. Qiu Jin, who had been working with the same network, was arrested and executed afterward. Before Married women had no separate legal self, and abolition trained the organizers Under English common law, a married woman’s legal identity was absorbed into her husband’s. The doctrine is called coverture. Her property, her contracts, and her wages belonged to him unless a statute carved out an exception. An unmarried woman had more legal room. Marriage closed it. In the United States, states began to pass Married Women’s Property Acts in the 1840s — New York’s 1848 statute is the usual example — but those laws were limited, uneven, and did not make a wife a full legal person. Industrial work had already left the house. What remained, for middle-class white women, was a public story about respectability: the home as a moral refuge, the woman as domestic, delicate, and good. Historians call this “separate spheres.” It was a rule of class as much as of sex. Enslaved women, and women who worked for wages, were never offered that protected private role. They were already in public as labor, as property, or as exceptions the ideology did not have to explain. Abolition was the training ground for many United States feminists. In anti-slavery societies they learned to petition legislatures, lecture to mixed audiences, edit newspapers, and run a meeting. Those skills transferred to women’s rights. The alliance later cracked, after the Civil War, when the question became which emancipation would be allowed to go first: Black men’s suffrage, or women’s. The era Seneca Falls, the Fifteenth Amendment split, and the 1913 parade On 19–20 July 1848, at Seneca Falls, New York, a convention issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. Elizabeth Cady Stanton was the principal author; Lucretia Mott was among the organizers. The vote was one grievance among others — property, divorce, education, and public speech. Not everyone in the room wanted the vote named first. The document still did something new in American public life: it treated women as people who could claim the same political rights the United States had already claimed for men. A 1908 souvenir card titled “Our Roll of Honor,” printed sixty years after Seneca Falls, listing the women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments. Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton head the first column. This is a commemorative card, not the 1848 manuscript. Printed souvenir card titled Our Roll of Honor, listing women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments. In 1851 Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from Frances Dana Gage’s 1863 rewrite of that speech. Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. The later version is the one that traveled in print. The historical point does not depend on the catchphrase. A feminism built on white middle-class delicacy treated enslaved women and working women as exceptions — people whose bodies had already been asked to do too much to count as the “woman” the movement was picturing. After the Civil War the coalition split over the Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, which barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. In 1869 Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony founded the National Woman Suffrage Association and opposed ratifying the amendment without women. Lucy Stone and others founded the American Woman Suffrage Association and would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait. Frederick Douglass, who had supported women’s rights at Seneca Falls, took Stone’s side on sequence. The argument was about order, and about who was being asked to stand aside. The two organizations did not merge into the National American Woman Suffrage Association until 1890. In Britain the movement divided by method. Constitutional suffragists collected signatures and lobbied Parliament. The militant Women’s Social and Political Union, founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst, broke windows, disrupted meetings, and, in prison, went on hunger strike. The Liberal government answered with force-feeding, then with the 1913 Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Act — the “Cat and Mouse Act” — which released weakened prisoners and rearrested them when they recovered. In June 1913 Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby in front of the king’s horse. Emmeline Pankhurst in 1913, the year Emily Wilding Davison died at Epsom and the Women’s Social and Political Union’s militancy was impossible to ignore. Constitutional suffragists were still collecting signatures. Pankhurst’s organization was collecting prison sentences. Formal seated portrait of Emmeline Pankhurst, 1913. On 3 March 1913, the day before Wilson’s inauguration, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized the Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C. Inez Milholland rode in white on a white horse at the head of the line. Black women were told to march in a rear contingent. Ida B. Wells refused. She waited until the Illinois delegation passed, then stepped into that line and marched with her state. The crowd on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913. Men climbed poles and wagons to see. Alice Paul timed the procession for the eve of Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration so it could not be missed. Being unmissable was not the same as being welcomed: spectators repeatedly stepped into the street and broke the line of march. A dense crowd lining Pennsylvania Avenue to watch the 1913 woman suffrage procession in Washington, D.C. The official program for the same day. The horse, the banner, and the Capitol show who the procession wanted to look like. Ida B. Wells’s decision to leave the “rear contingent” and walk with the Illinois delegation is the part the program does not print. Color official program cover for the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913, showing a woman on horseback before the Capitol. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not repeal Jim Crow. Many Black women in the South were still blocked by poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence. The amendment changed the federal text. The local machinery that decided who could actually cast a ballot did not change with it. The same years, in a different country: Qiu Jin 秋瑾 (1875–1907). She unbound her feet, left an arranged marriage, studied in Japan from 1904, and in 1907 edited 中國女報 (the Chinese Women’s Journal) in Shanghai. The journal argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same pages as anti-Qing politics. After Xu Xilin’s uprising in Anqing failed, she was arrested and executed. Her public life does not sit on a line from Seneca Falls to 1920. It belongs in the same decades anyway: a woman deciding she would count in public, under a different state, and paying for it with her life. People Four people the usual story has to include Sojourner Truth c. 1797–1883 Born enslaved in New York. She sold cartes-de-visite captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” The card was a living: lectures did not pay enough, and she needed the sales. It was also a legal claim. She copyrighted the image in her own name, which was unusual for a sitter, and still more unusual for a woman who had been treated as property. Carte-de-visite, 1864, printed with her own line: “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” Ida B. Wells 1862–1931 Anti-lynching journalist; Southern Horrors appeared in 1892. She treated suffrage and racial terror as one fight, which is why a segregated parade order in 1913 was not a small slight. She refused the rear contingent and walked into the Illinois line as it passed. Ida B. Wells-Barnett, photographed by Mary Garrity around 1893. Inez Milholland 1886–1916 Lawyer, and the image the 1913 procession needed at its head. She died in 1916 on a western suffrage tour, at thirty. The photograph of her on the white horse outlived the campaign she was riding for. Milholland on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913: white cape, white horse, a planned public image. Qiu Jin 秋瑾 1875–1907 Unbound feet, study in Japan, editor of 中國女報, executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. If the phrase “first wave” cannot hold her, the phrase is too narrow. Her life is not the problem. Qiu Jin, photographed between 1900 and 1907, in the last years of the Qing dynasty. A story “I sell the shadow to support the substance” Sojourner Truth, 1864. She sold the card because lectures did not pay enough. She also put her own copyright on it. Sojourner Truth’s 1864 carte-de-visite, with the printed line I sell the shadow to support the substance under her portrait. Truth sold her image because lectures did not pay enough. On the card, the “shadow” is the photograph — a thing that can be reproduced, captioned, and passed from hand to hand. The “substance” is the work, and the body that had been treated as property. She put the sentence on the card in English, under her own name, and made the sale part of the argument: I will be paid for the copy of me that you can hold. Keep the card in mind when a movement talks about “women” as if the category were already settled. Someone is always deciding which body is the subject of the campaign, and which body is only used to illustrate it. After After 1920 the coalition thinned, and a later generation named a second wave In the United States the 1920s through the 1950s are often called the “doldrums”: the vote arrived, and the suffrage coalition thinned. The word is a later summary, not a name people used at the time. It describes a particular organized feminism going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended, and it does not mean every woman had been in that coalition. What later writers called the second wave — the 1960s and 1970s — turned to the workplace, to sexuality, and to housework. “The personal is political” became a slogan for that turn. The who-counts problem returned in public, including in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977, which refused to treat race, sex, and class as separate queues. The wave metaphor itself is a later teaching device. It offers a tidy sequence: first the vote, then the rest. It hides the people who were never in that sequence — and the fights that did not wait for the next numbered period. A question A question to keep asking When a movement says “we,” who is being asked to wait? Time to Remember — Time of the Suffragettes (1911–1913) British Pathé compilation of British suffragette newsreel, 1911–1913. This is not film of the 1913 Washington procession. The Derby — 1912 & 1913 British Pathé racing newsreel. It includes the 1913 Epsom Derby, when Emily Wilding Davison stepped onto the course. Again: Britain, not Pennsylvania Avenue.
